- **Gaussian-decay overclaim:** Ramsey decay under Gaussian quasistatic 1/f noise can be approximately Gaussian with
  logarithmic corrections. Non-Gaussian fluctuators/cutoffs/coupling sweet spots yield other forms.
- **DD gain:** Additional pulses reshape the filter but do not buy a universal factor of bandwidth suppression; pulse
  error and high-frequency noise create an optimum.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** A scale-free bath is conceptually intriguing and explains why measured coherence depends on
  observation protocol.

#### §18.3 — Markovian versus non-Markovian paragraph

- **Classical definition too strong:** Markov processes need conditional future independence given the present, not
  unconditional statistical independence at all separated times. Finite bath correlation time supports an
  approximation, not the literal statement given.
- **Quantum definitions:** CP-divisibility, semigroup dynamics, information backflow, and process-tensor memory are
  inequivalent notions of quantum Markovianity. Choose one operational definition.
- **Lindblad nuance:** Time-homogeneous GKSL generators yield semigroups; time-local Lindblad-form equations with
  time-dependent nonnegative rates can be CP-divisible and nonexponential.
- **Strong characterization defect:** Markovian decoherence is not always purely single-exponential or completely
  described by one constant rate; multilevel/multiple Lindblad operators yield several modes.
- **Simulation:** Fresh stochastic samples represent some classical Markov noise, not arbitrary quantum Markov channels;
  Kraus trajectories may be sampled with state-dependent jumps.
- **1/f:** Long correlations make 1/f noise a standard non-Markovian/quasistatic example, but the formal label depends on
  system timescale and definition.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Memory across gates is intuitive, though the formal simplification is too aggressive.

#### §18.3 — information backflow

- **One witness, not universal signature:** Revival of trace distance between an optimized pair of states is the
  Breuer–Laine–Piilo information-backflow criterion. Some non-Markovian dynamics under other definitions show no such
  revival, so “the practical signature” and “regularly” overclaim.
- **Tomographic burden:** Detecting backflow requires state pairs, time-resolved tomography, SPAM control, and
  statistical significance; it is not a simple routine diagnostic.
- **Physical revivals:** Oscillations can arise from coherent system modes, calibration drift, or finite environments;
  model selection remains necessary.
- **Markov statement:** CP-divisible dynamics contract trace distance, but positive-divisible/noninvertible subtleties
  deserve care if making a theorem-level assertion.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Lost distinguishability returning is a vivid way to make environmental memory tangible.

#### §18.3 — circuit accumulation example

- **Arithmetic:** `$1-0.999^{1000}\approx0.6323$`, so 63% follows if “fidelity” composes as independent survival
  probabilities.
- **Model defect:** Average gate fidelity does not generally multiply into end-to-end success this way; depolarizing
  parameters, observable, coherent error, dimension, and circuit structure determine composition.
- **Correlated-noise direction:** Slow coherent drift can accumulate quadratically/worst-case faster, but can also
  cancel, refocus, or produce circuit-dependent bias. It is false that correlated 1/f noise necessarily accumulates
  faster at the same reported fidelity.
- **Benchmark mismatch:** A fidelity averaged over random sequences/time may hide drift, but long-circuit prediction
  requires process tensors, cycle errors, context dependence, or repeated calibration—not a single 0.999.
- **Useful lesson:** The benchmarking-to-application gap is important; replace the numeric survival heuristic with a
  simulated coherent-overrotation versus stochastic-Pauli example.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** The 63% number is memorable, but its simplistic multiplication risks becoming the wrong rule
  readers retain.

#### §18.4 — decoherence-limited error opening

- **Scaling:** Infidelity is linear in gate duration over coherence time at short times, but coefficients depend on
  amplitude damping/dephasing and average-versus-worst-case metric. `$\epsilon\sim t_{\rm gate}/T$` is an order-of-
  magnitude heuristic only.
- **Transmon arithmetic:** 20–50 ns over 100 µs is roughly `$2\times10^{-4}$` to `$5\times10^{-4}$`, so “around
  `$10^{-4}$`” is optimistic unless metric coefficients or longer T are included.
- **T1/T2 combination:** Use an average-gate-infidelity formula incorporating both relaxation and pure dephasing rather
  than a single unspecified `$T$`.
- **Ion range:** 1–100 µs spans one- and two-qubit gates and technologies; comparing “the same gate” is inaccurate.
- **Strong unit error:** “achieve `$10^{-4}$` to `$10^{-5}$` per-gate fidelity” must mean error/infidelity. Fidelity
  would be 0.9999–0.99999.
- **Causal conclusion:** If measured error exceeds the coherence-limit estimate, control, motion/heating, crosstalk,
  SPAM contamination, or model mismatch may dominate; it does not identify control noise uniquely.
- **Current numbers:** All platform values need dated sources and matched gate types/protocols.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Converting coherence times into a gate-error floor is exactly the calculation practitioners
  need, once units and coefficients are repaired.

#### §18.4 — control-limited errors

- **Rotation example:** A multiplicative 1% amplitude error gives the stated `$R_X(1.01\pi)$` only for a linear
  pulse-area/rotation calibration and negligible distortion/detuning.
- **Metric opportunity:** The coherent angle error is `$\delta=\pi/100$`, while average infidelity is quadratic in
  `$\delta$` (about `$\delta^2/6$` for a single-qubit unitary error under one convention) and worst-case coherent error
  scales linearly. Computing both would perfectly motivate §18.10.
- **Systematic qualifier:** Amplitude/phase/shape errors may drift or fluctuate; only stable miscalibration is the same
  coherent overrotation every application.
- **Axis errors:** Phase error changes rotation axis, detuning adds a Z component, and waveform distortion is not always
  representable as a simple angle rescaling.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The extra-rotation picture is crisp and naturally sets up coherent accumulation.

#### §18.4 — leakage/crosstalk pointer

- **Too thin:** A one-line pointer is acceptable after §18.1, but “quantifiable as a separate component” promises an
  additive error-budget decomposition that context-dependent leakage/crosstalk may not permit.
- **Section roles:** §18.13 appears to benchmark simultaneous/cycle behavior rather than uniquely separate causal
  components; make that limitation explicit.
- **Entertainment: 2/5.** Pure navigation.

#### §18.4 — 2023–2025 single-qubit fidelity ranges

- **Primary-source audit:** “Best-in-class,” platform ranges, years, qubit count, gate duration, simultaneous versus
  isolated operation, and uncertainty must be sourced to comparable primary experiments.
- **Metric mismatch:** “Single-qubit Clifford gates” may mean Clifford RB error per Clifford, error per primitive gate,
  or interleaved RB for a target gate. These are not interchangeable.
- **Selection bias:** Record fidelities on selected qubits do not describe device-wide medians/yields needed for
  algorithms or QEC.
- **Neutral-atom spread:** Atom loss, rearrangement, local/global addressing, and which logical clock/Raman gate strongly
  affect the number.
- **Temporal language:** A fixed 2023–2025 snapshot should not say “where the field stands today.”
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Cross-platform numbers are compelling, but only if the comparison table is disciplined.

#### §18.4 — two-qubit fidelity ranges

- **Gate heterogeneity:** CZ, CNOT, Mølmer–Sørensen, and Rydberg CZ have different durations, connectivity, calibration,
  leakage/loss conventions, and reported metrics. A single ranked list can mislead.
- **“Latest/most current”:** These are temporally unstable, undefined populations; use dated record and representative
  medians.
- **Evered citation:** Verify whether 99.5% is raw, SPAM-corrected, randomized-benchmarking-derived, postselected against
  atom loss, and on how many atom pairs.
- **“Successors exceeded”:** Name the papers and exact comparable number; otherwise this is unverifiable hearsay.
- **QEC relevance:** Simultaneous full-cycle error, leakage, correlated faults, measurement/reset, and yield matter more
  than isolated two-qubit average fidelity.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** The platform race is intrinsically interesting and exceptionally easy to misreport.

#### §18.4 — measurement and idle ranges

- **Measurement:** Assignment fidelity needs definition (average of conditional correct probabilities), integration
  time, QND/repeatability, leakage/loss handling, and simultaneous-readout crosstalk.
- **Idle-unit error:** “`$10^{-4}$ per microsecond” is inconsistent with `$T\sim100\,\mu$s`; the raw short-time ratio is
  roughly 1% per microsecond, with average-infidelity coefficients still around several `$10^{-3}$`, not `$10^{-4}$`.
  This is a strong numerical defect unless the statement refers to much longer coherence or a special decoupled idle.
- **Platform contradiction:** On long-coherence ions/atoms idle errors may be tiny per microsecond, while on transmons
  the stated universal range is untenable.
- **Idle context:** DD pulses, spectator couplings, frequency parking, thermal excitation, and scheduling affect idle
  error beyond `$T_1/T_2$`.
- **Entertainment: 3/5.** Useful categories, but the idle figure materially distorts the budget.

#### §18.4 — claimed two-qubit bottleneck and code scaling

- **Universal bottleneck defect:** Measurement/reset, leakage, idle/dephasing, crosstalk, feed-forward, loss, and factory
  operations can bottleneck fault tolerance depending on platform and code.
- **“Decade of fidelity”:** Fidelity is near one; the intended phrase is likely a tenfold reduction in two-qubit
  infidelity/error rate.
- **No direct translation:** Surface-code distance depends nonlinearly/logarithmically on target logical error and on
  physical error relative to threshold; a tenfold physical-error reduction does not universally map directly to a
  fixed patch-size reduction.
- **Noise model:** Biased/correlated/leakage errors with the same average infidelity can yield very different thresholds
  and patches.
- **Cross-reference:** §19.12 should supply the actual logical-error fit and assumptions before this claim.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The QEC consequence raises the stakes, but “directly” conceals the most important modeling.

#### §18.4 — infidelity versus error-per-gate

- **Good warning:** Average benchmarking numbers are not worst-case channel guarantees.
- **RB conversion:** Standard Clifford RB estimates a decay parameter under assumptions; average error per Clifford is
  related by a dimension-dependent factor and extracting primitive-gate error requires further modeling. It does not
  simply “return average gate error approximating the depolarising parameter.”
- **Noise dependence:** Gate-dependent, non-Markovian, leakage, and time-dependent noise complicate the fitted decay and
  interpretation.
- **Worst-case example:** A 0.1% average infidelity can permit diamond distance on the order of its square root for
  coherent errors, so a percent-scale worst case is plausible; derive/bound it rather than asserting one chosen number.
- **Diamond metric:** Diamond distance is operationally natural for worst-case channel distinguishability including an
  ancilla, but “proper” is value-laden; unitarity, leakage, Pauli rates, and application-specific metrics also matter.
- **Measurement difficulty:** Direct diamond estimation is generally tomography-hard and GST estimates retain gauge/
  model issues; the lack of standardized reporting is real but needs a standards source.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Revealing what a string of nines can hide is excellent practitioner education.

#### §18.5 — readout framing

- **Strong oversimplification:** Readout error is not merely noise on a returned classical bit. The quantum measurement
  instrument includes assignment, backaction, state transition, leakage/loss, spectator disturbance, and post-
  measurement state.
- **End-of-circuit scope:** For destructive terminal measurement, a classical confusion matrix may suffice for some
  tasks; mid-circuit/QEC requires the full instrument/QND properties.
- **Cross-reference:** Verify §11.7 distinguishes assignment correction from physical measurement mitigation and
  correlated multi-qubit readout.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The classical-bit framing is accessible but too narrow for the mid-circuit discussion.

#### §18.5 — four conditional probabilities

- **Matrix language:** These are the four entries of a binary assignment matrix, not “corners” in a standard technical
  term; the metaphor is harmless.
- **Complementarity:** `$P(1|0)=1-P(0|0)$` and `$P(0|1)=1-P(1|1)$` only if every shot receives exactly one binary
  assignment and loss/leakage/erasure outcomes are folded into it.
- **Preparation contamination:** Calibration estimates combine preparation and measurement error unless heralding or a
  joint model separates them.
- **Current percentages:** “Usually 99%+” and 1–3% asymmetry require dated device distributions and simultaneous versus
  isolated measurement conditions.
- **Physical mechanisms:** T1 during integration is important for superconducting excited-state assignment, but
  overlapping IQ clouds, thermal excitation, measurement-induced transitions, leakage, and classifier bias also
  contribute.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The 2×2 table is intuitive and should be displayed visually.

#### §18.5 — asymmetry and integration tradeoff

- **Platform qualifier:** The text appropriately scopes the physical statement to superconducting hardware, though it
  still is not universal for every device/operating point.
- **Signal integration:** Longer integration can improve separation only until resonator dynamics, nonstationarity,
  state transitions, amplifier noise, and matched-filter choice set an optimum.
- **T1 probability:** For a qubit initially excited throughout a 1 µs interval with 100 µs T1,
  `$1-e^{-0.01}\approx0.995\%$`; the arithmetic is sound as a raw event probability.
- **Assignment mapping:** Not every decay event causes misclassification; timing within the integration and classifier
  weighting matter. Conversely other errors occur without decay.
- **Q-factor claim:** Reaching 0.1% is not simply a hardware Q-factor problem. Faster resonator depletion, Purcell
  filtering, parametric amplification, optimal filters/classifiers, latching/cycling schemes, and better T1 all matter;
  increasing resonator Q can slow response.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** The competing benefits of waiting longer make a memorable design tradeoff.

#### §18.5 — mid-circuit measurement

- **Protocol dependence:** A mid-circuit measurement need not reset the measured qubit; QND measurement ideally leaves
  it in the measured eigenstate, and explicit reset is added only when required.
- **Spectators:** Measurement-induced dephasing, resonator photons, frequency collisions, optical scattering, and
  classical crosstalk need platform-specific treatment.
- **Latency budget:** Feed-forward must beat the relevant logical schedule/coherence/error-correction cycle, not always
  the bare physical `$T_2$`.
- **Quality metrics:** Include assignment fidelity, QNDness/repeatability, leakage, reset fidelity/time, spectator error,
  erasure flagging, and conditional-operation latency.
- **“Leading frontier”:** Time-sensitive and broad; cite platform roadmaps/experiments or state it as a challenge.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The measurement becoming an active control operation effectively raises the engineering stakes.

#### §18.6 — state-preparation framing

- **Subdominance overclaim:** State preparation can dominate algorithms needing pure ancillas, repeated mid-circuit
  reset, postselection, photonic sources, atom loading, or error-detection. Scope the claim to terminal-circuit
  transmon initialization.
- **Mechanisms incomplete:** Pulse mispreparation, leakage, optical pumping error, atom/ion loss, imperfect cooling, and
  correlated initialization also matter.
- **Definition:** Preparation infidelity should be stated relative to the intended density operator and include
  correlations across qubits.
- **Entertainment: 3/5.** Useful but platform-narrow.

#### §18.6 — residual population

- **Current range:** `$10^{-3}$–$10^{-2}$` residual excitation is plausible for some transmons but needs dates, qubit
  frequencies, filtering, measurement technique, and whether active/heralded initialization was used.
- **Notation defect:** Calling the observed nonequilibrium population `$p_1^{\rm eq}$` contradicts §18.1, which explains
  that it exceeds the fridge-equilibrium prediction. Use `$p_1^{\rm ss}$` or effective-thermal population.
- **Two-level approximation:** Real initialization includes `$|2\rangle$` and higher-state population; the displayed
  mixture may be incomplete.
- **Correlations:** Quasiparticle/cosmic events can correlate initial excitations across qubits; a product of single-
  qubit thermal mixtures is not assured.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The many-orders mismatch from naive fridge equilibrium remains a strong hardware lesson.

#### §18.6 — active reset

- **Protocol:** Measure-and-conditional-X is clear, but latency, classifier confidence, QNDness, and post-measurement
  transitions determine performance.
- **T1 direction error:** A T1 event after a correct X-to-zero helps rather than harms; decay between measurement and a
  conditional X can cause the pulse to re-excite the qubit. Thermal upward events and readout misassignment also matter.
- **Error addition:** Residual reset error is not simply measurement error “plus” T1; conditional branches and repeated
  rounds require a transition model.
- **Numbers:** `$10^{-3}$–`$10^{-4}$` after 2–3 rounds and percent after one require primary data and matched duration;
  repeated rounds can saturate or add heating/leakage.
- **“Heralded”:** A conditional reset is not automatically heralded unless an additional verification measurement
  accepts/rejects the result.
- **Unconditional reset:** Resonator-assisted/dissipative reset protocols vary and can induce spectator error; comparable
  numbers need sources.
- **Cross-reference:** Verify §21.9 contains reset rather than a platform-specific section mismatch.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Feedback reset is an intuitive miniature control loop, and the branching errors merit a
  diagram.

#### §18.6 — SPAM inseparability, RB, and GST

- **Identifiability:** A single prepare–gate–measure probability indeed cannot uniquely assign error among preparation,
  transformation, and measurement without assumptions.
- **RB robustness:** Constant SPAM changes RB fit amplitude/offset rather than decay under the standard model; sequence-
  dependent SPAM, drift, leakage, and gate dependence can still bias fits. “SPAM-robust” needs this scope.
- **GST:** Gate-set tomography jointly estimates preparation, measurement, and gates self-consistently, but gauge freedom
  prevents a unique separation without a gauge choice and Markov/model assumptions.
- **Strong subtraction defect:** In many analyses one cannot simply subtract a combined SPAM contribution from gate
  metrics. RB fits nuisance parameters; GST models all components; neither licenses generic subtraction.
- **Acronym:** Expanding SPAM is useful, but avoid implying state preparation and measurement are physically one error
  class merely because they are statistically confounded.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The identifiability problem is subtle and important, and the competing benchmark strategies
  make it concrete.

#### §18.7 — crosstalk definition

- **Definition breadth:** Cross-qubit effects from control/measurement are crosstalk; effects on the same qubit’s
  leakage levels are control leakage/spectral leakage, not naturally “cross” talk.
- **Static coupling:** An always-on interaction can produce context dependence even without an active operation; include
  it explicitly rather than tying definition only to operations.
- **Classical/quantum split:** The labels can blur because classical drive leakage produces coherent quantum evolution
  and quantum coupling is controlled by classical pulses. A source-versus-mediated-interaction taxonomy is clearer.
- **Entertainment: 3/5.** Functional but repeats §18.1.

#### §18.7 — classical crosstalk

- **“Same wire”:** Separate control lines can couple through package modes, electronics, microwave launchers, or optical
  spillover; same-wire fanout is only one architecture.
- **Coupling language:** Capacitive/inductive coupling describes hardware paths, while a control field’s leak may be
  electromagnetic transfer rather than direct circuit coupling.
- **Mitigation overclaim:** Linear precompensation works for stable, measurable transfer matrices but not arbitrary
  nonlinear, frequency-dependent, state-dependent, drifting, or saturating crosstalk.
- **Calibration cost:** Measuring a full crosstalk matrix scales poorly and simultaneous pulses create pair/higher-order
  context not captured independently.
- **“Never exactly zero”:** Physically plausible but unnecessary absolute; below measurable/relevant tolerance is the
  engineering objective.
- **Entertainment: 3/5.** Clear, though overly schematic.

#### §18.7 — quantum/ZZ crosstalk

- **Mechanism:** Static residual ZZ coupling gives spectator-state-dependent conditional phases and is an important
  superconducting error.
- **Normalization:** Depending on Hamiltonian convention the term may be `$\zeta Z_iZ_j/2$` or `/4`; define `$\zeta$`
  before translating to phase.
- **“Entire time”:** Correct for a constant interaction in the lab/rotating frame, but echo sequences and commuting
  phases can cancel/track it.
- **Tunable couplers:** Residual off-state coupling, flux noise, calibration, parasitic direct coupling, and coupler
  leakage prevent generic “nearly zero” guarantees.
- **ZZ-free points:** Frequency parking may introduce collisions, dephasing, or reduced gateability; note tradeoffs.
- **Platform scope:** Shared motional modes/optical fields generate different quantum crosstalk on ions/atoms.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The invisible spectator-dependent phase is a strong concrete example.

#### §18.7 — crosstalk and QEC

- **Strong assumption defect:** Surface-code fault tolerance does not require all operations/errors to be independent;
  threshold theorems tolerate sufficiently local, bounded correlated noise under specified models. Many simple decoders
  assume independent Pauli priors, which is a different claim.
- **Decoder claim:** A decoder can incorporate pairwise/correlated edge models or learned/contextual noise; “cannot
  interpret” is false for standard extensions and too broad even for matching decoders.
- **Numeric transformation:** A 0.5% physical rate becoming “effectively 1.5%” under nearest-neighbor ZZ has no defined
  metric, coupling strength, schedule, decoder, or source. Remove or provide a full cited simulation.
- **Threshold:** There is no single surface-code threshold; it depends on circuit/noise/decoder/measurement/leakage and
  may be far below/above 1% under different assumptions.
- **Diagnostic:** Simultaneous RB detects context-dependent average decay but does not uniquely quantify QEC-cycle
  correlated faults; cycle benchmarking/correlation spectroscopy may be more relevant.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Crosstalk threatening exponential logical suppression is compelling, but unsupported numbers
  manufacture drama.

#### §18.8 — leakage mechanisms

- **Definition repetition:** Repeats §18.1 nearly verbatim; consolidate the overview there and reserve this section for
  quantitative models/diagnostics.
- **Higher-level wording:** Leakage can go to lower/nonordered states, loss, or noncomputational manifolds; retain
  platform-general subspace language.
- **Transmon CZ:** Avoided-crossing CZ implementations can intentionally approach/hybridize `$|11\rangle$` and
  `$|20\rangle$`, but modern CZ families differ (tunable couplers, parametric, microwave-activated). Do not imply all
  transmon CZ gates use this path.
- **Ion analogy:** Off-resonant hyperfine leakage, motional excitation, and spontaneous emission are distinct; specify
  which counts as internal-state leakage.
- **Neutral atoms:** Residual Rydberg population may decay, be lost, or remain temporarily outside the computational
  manifold; atom loss often deserves an erasure category.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Platform comparisons are helpful despite repetition.

#### §18.8 — leakage danger

- **Syndrome behavior:** A leaked qubit may yield anomalous/random/repeated syndrome patterns, not simply “look like an
  ordinary error.” Its interaction-dependent propagation is the key distinction.
- **Lifetime claim:** `$|2\rangle$` lifetime can be shorter or related by oscillator matrix elements to computational
  T1; “often longer” needs evidence and may be wrong for transmons.
- **Persistence:** What matters is lifetime relative to QEC cycle and reset cadence, not bare `$T_1$` alone.
- **Empirical superlative:** “Single largest contributor” to time-correlated error across surface-code experiments is
  current, platform-specific, and likely unsupported universally. Cite named experiments.
- **Other correlations:** Cosmic rays, drift, residual couplings, measurement resonators, and decoder/model effects can
  dominate.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** A fault persisting across rounds is an effective explanation of why leakage is worse than a
  one-cycle Pauli error.

#### §18.8 — gate-level mitigation

- **DRAG:** Derivative-removal-by-adiabatic-gate pulses suppress leakage/phase errors for weakly anharmonic systems, but
  improvement is device/calibration dependent; “order of magnitude over square pulses” needs a cited setup.
- **Baseline:** Modern gates rarely use raw square pulses, making that comparison pedagogically historical rather than a
  current performance claim.
- **Ion STIRAP:** Verify that STIRAP-like protocols are a standard leakage-mitigation analogue for the ion gates in
  scope; pulse shaping, polarization, detuning, and repumping may be more representative.
- **Tradeoff:** Leakage suppression can increase duration or phase/control error; optimize total error, not leakage alone.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Pulse shape as subspace containment is intuitive.

#### §18.8 — circuit-level LRUs

- **“Pump back” danger:** Returning population from leakage does not generally restore the unknown logical state that
  existed before leakage; an LRU converts leakage into a located/unlocated computational error that QEC must correct.
- **Swap-and-reset:** A SWAP involving a leaked multilevel qubit is not an ideal qubit SWAP and can propagate leakage.
  Surface-code role-swapping/teleportation schemes need explicit leakage-aware gates.
- **Fresh ancilla cost:** Requires qubits, routing, reset, and fault-tolerant scheduling; ancilla may itself leak.
- **Period selection:** Too frequent LRUs add errors, too rare allow correlated propagation; this is an error-budget
  optimization.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The architectural response is useful, but “simplest” conceals a nontrivial leakage-aware
  operation.

#### §18.8 — decoder-level mitigation

- **Detection:** Syndrome streaks can indicate leakage but are not unique; persistent data errors, measurement faults,
  or crosstalk can look similar.
- **Decoder action:** A classical decoder cannot physically reset a qubit by itself; detection must trigger a controller/
  circuit operation and update the Pauli/frame/erasure information.
- **Information:** Direct leakage-sensitive readout or erasure flags can greatly improve decoding; include these
  alternatives.
- **Model:** Hidden-Markov, correlated matching, belief propagation, or learned decoders can model persistence; name one
  concrete approach.
- **False positives:** Resetting a nonleaked data qubit destroys state unless done through a fault-tolerant replacement/
  teleportation protocol.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** A temporal syndrome signature makes decoding feel like diagnosis rather than bookkeeping.

#### §18.8 — fault-tolerance theorem claim

- **Strong theorem overgeneralization:** Threshold theorems assume particular local noise models; some explicitly extend
  to leakage with leakage-reduction constructions. They do not share one premise “leakage suppressed below the
  threshold.”
- **Threshold dimension:** Leakage rate alone is insufficient; propagation strength, duration, locality, LRU error, and
  conversion to regular faults determine an effective threshold.
- **Precondition/consequence:** Fault-tolerant gadgets can themselves contain leakage, so mitigation is part of the
  construction rather than wholly prior to the theorem.
- **Chapter 19:** State the exact theorem/noise model to be taught there and align the wording.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** It correctly signals leakage cannot be ignored, but presents folklore as a universal theorem.

#### §18.9 — GAD Kraus operators

- **Algebra:** The four displayed operators form a trace-preserving generalized amplitude-damping channel under the
  stated convention, with downward branch weight `$p$` and upward branch weight `$1-p$`.
- **Parameter convention:** Textbooks sometimes define `$p$` as the ground-state equilibrium population and sometimes
  swap branch labels. Explicitly verify `$\sum K_i^\dagger K_i=I$` and the fixed point to lock the convention.
- **Finite-temperature T1:** `$\gamma=1-e^{-t/T_1}$` is valid when measured `$T_1^{-1}=\Gamma_\downarrow+\Gamma_\uparrow$`
  is the population-relaxation rate. It is not literally the zero-temperature downward rate reused unchanged.
- **Semigroup condition:** For a fixed thermal bath, upward/downward rates satisfy detailed balance; arbitrary
  time-dependent `$\gamma,p$` may not form a semigroup.
- **Higher levels:** The qubit GAD channel ignores transmon `$|2\rangle$` population and leakage, important at the
  precision this chapter discusses.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The upward Kraus operator makes finite temperature operationally clear.

#### §18.9 — zero-temperature limit and fixed point

- **Limit:** At `$p=1$`, `$K_2,K_3$` vanish and ordinary downward amplitude damping remains; correct.
- **Fixed point:** The stated diagonal state with excited population `$1-p$` is correct for nonzero damping under this
  convention.
- **Equilibrium notation:** Use `$p_1^{\rm eq}$` only for a genuine/model-effective thermal fixed point; nonequilibrium
  quasiparticle populations may not obey detailed balance.
- **Readout asymmetry causal claim:** Downward transitions during integration contribute to worse excited-state
  assignment, but finite bath temperature is not the sole origin; even a zero-temperature bath gives downward T1
  asymmetry. Saying it has “the same origin” incorrectly makes nonzero T essential.
- **Idle statement:** Correct within the stationary GAD model; active drives, quasiparticle bursts, leakage, and reset
  make real idle fixed points more complex.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** A non-ground fixed point is a useful correction to the default damping picture.

#### §18.9 — budget contribution and characterization

- **Unsupported percentage:** “1–10% of total error” has no defined device, operation, metric, or decomposition and
  cannot be universal across current cryogenic platforms.
- **“Dominates only when”:** Thermal excitation can dominate initialization/readout even when control/dephasing remain
  substantial; contribution depends on task and idling.
- **Temperature inference:** A single `$p_1$` and transition frequency yields an effective two-level temperature only if
  detailed-balance/thermal assumptions hold. Measuring upward/downward rates is a stronger diagnostic.
- **Standard-suite claim:** Plausible but should cite measurement protocols and distinguish direct population,
  heralding bias, and readout correction.
- **Spelling:** “Characterisation” remains British; ensure consistency.
- **Entertainment: 3/5.** Practical, but the unsupported percentage adds false precision.

#### §18.10 — coherent-error definition and compounding

- **Definition:** A fixed unitary deviation is the canonical coherent error; a pure input remains pure under the
  erroneous unitary, as stated.
- **Input qualifier:** A mixed input remains mixed, and an actual gate can combine coherent miscalibration with
  stochastic noise; coherent/incoherent is a decomposition, not mutually exclusive device classes.
- **Strong compounding condition:** `$n\delta$` angle accumulation assumes the same commuting/aligned overrotation is
  repeated in a frame where intervening ideal gates do not rotate/cancel its axis. Generic circuits can scramble,
  echo, or amplify it differently.
- **Probability regime:** Wrong-outcome probability is sinusoidal and measurement/input dependent; it scales as
  `$O((n\delta)^2)$` only for small accumulated angle and a sensitive state/measurement.
- **Systematic versus quasistatic:** A slowly varying shot-to-shot offset may be coherent within a circuit but
  incoherent after ensemble averaging. This important middle regime should be named.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The extra-rotation picture is vivid, though the clean quadratic law needs its narrow regime.

#### §18.10 — incoherent-error definition and compounding

- **Definition breadth:** Nonunitary channels are reasonable examples, but a stochastic mixture of unitaries is
  incoherent at the ensemble level while each trajectory remains pure.
- **Strong purity defect:** Depolarization often reduces purity, but amplitude damping can *increase* purity by relaxing
  a mixed state toward `$|0\rangle$`; dephasing leaves Z-basis eigenstates pure. Purity does not generically decay as
  `$(1-p)^n$`.
- **“Mixes with probability”:** A channel parameter `$p$` has different meanings for depolarizing, dephasing, Pauli,
  erasure, and damping channels. Do not use one survival model for all.
- **Wrong outcome:** `$1-(1-p)^n\approx np$` is valid for independent catastrophic Bernoulli faults or a chosen survival
  observable, not arbitrary channel error.
- **Temporal independence:** The rule assumes identical independent Markovian noise; correlated stochastic noise can
  scale differently.
- **Entertainment: 3/5.** The simple contrast is useful but physically overgeneralized.

#### §18.10 — same-infidelity comparison

- **Coefficient omission:** For a unitary overrotation, average infidelity is proportional to `$\delta^2$` with
  dimension/axis-dependent coefficient, not exactly `$\epsilon=\delta^2$`.
- **Like-for-like metric:** A stochastic channel’s `$p$` is likewise not always equal to average infidelity. Convert both
  to average infidelity or diamond distance explicitly.
- **Worst-case versus typical:** Coherent error can produce quadratic short-time buildup in an aligned circuit, making
  average fidelity dangerously optimistic; randomized circuits may convert accumulation closer to linear without
  deliberate twirling.
- **Saturation:** `$n^2\delta^2$` cannot grow indefinitely beyond probability one and may oscillate/cancel.
- **“Formal version”:** Drift can be harmful, but drift is time variation whereas a fixed miscalibration is systematic;
  distinguish them.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** This is a highly memorable warning once expressed as a bounded, circuit-dependent example.

#### §18.10 — Pauli/Clifford twirling

- **Circuit description:** Randomized compiling dresses each logical gate/cycle with random Paulis and correction Paulis
  chosen so the ideal computation is unchanged. “Apply `$P$` and `$P^\dagger$` at the next layer” is insufficient when
  intervening gates conjugate Paulis.
- **Average versus instance:** Twirling converts the *ensemble-averaged* channel; each randomized circuit still has a
  coherent unitary realization/noise trajectory. Multiple random compilations and shots are required.
- **Strong channel defect:** Pauli twirling converts a channel into a Pauli channel, not generally a fully depolarizing
  channel. Clifford twirling produces depolarizing form under the relevant gate-independent averaging assumptions.
- **Infidelity preservation:** Exact twirling preserves entanglement/average fidelity for an ideal group average, but
  imperfect randomizing gates, gate dependence, compilation, and finite sampling can change the implemented error.
- **Scaling promise:** Randomized compiling can tailor coherent errors into stochastic Pauli noise and improve worst-
  case accumulation; it does not universally guarantee exact `$n^2\to n$` application-error conversion.
- **RB relation:** Clifford twirling/2-design averaging motivates standard RB, but RB’s sequence-dependent noise
  analysis is more nuanced than a literal physical twirl of one fixed channel.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Intentionally randomizing a device to make it more predictable is delightfully
  counterintuitive.

#### §18.10 — Bloch-sphere picture

- **Coherent picture:** A one-qubit unitary error preserves Bloch-vector length and shifts orientation; correct.
- **Depolarizing picture:** Isotropic depolarization shrinks toward the origin. Dephasing shrinks transverse components,
  and amplitude damping both contracts and translates toward the ground-state pole; include these contrasts.
- **Twirled ensemble:** Clifford-twirled average noise gives symmetric shrinkage, but individual runs are not physically
  shortened Bloch vectors merely by applying perfect random unitaries.
- **“Same length loss”:** A unitary error has no physical purity/length loss before averaging; the shrinkage reflects
  uncertainty over randomized frames, while average fidelity is retained. Rephrase to avoid implying literal
  decoherence was present.
- **Figure opportunity:** A three-panel Bloch diagram (fixed overrotation, dephasing ellipse, ensemble depolarization)
  would materially help.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** This is the section’s clearest intuition.

#### §18.10 — benchmarking implications

- **RB output:** Standard RB estimates an average decay parameter under assumptions, not an unconditional “average
  error rate.”
- **Insensitive overclaim:** Coherent and stochastic channels can share average fidelity/RB decay, but coherent errors
  affect sequence-to-sequence variance, nonexponential behavior, gate dependence, and unitarity. RB alone usually
  cannot identify the decomposition; “insensitive” is too absolute.
- **Cycle benchmarking:** It estimates Pauli fidelities/errors for a twirled cycle and can expose context, but is not by
  itself the generic coherent-versus-incoherent discriminator claimed.
- **Purity/unitarity benchmarking:** Purity benchmarking estimates unitarity/incoherence through second moments or
  purity-sensitive measurements, not simply “residual purity of the output state.”
- **Other tools:** GST, robust phase estimation, repeated-gate amplification, and error-amplification sequences can
  diagnose coherent errors.
- **Cross-reference:** Ensure §18.13’s actual protocol supports every promised distinction.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** It turns an abstract distinction into a clear reason not to trust one benchmark number.

#### §18.11 — section premise

- **Overstatement:** Markovian white stationary noise is a deliberately simple baseline, but “rarely accurate” needs a
  timescale and accuracy target. Effective Markovian models can predict many calibrated circuits adequately.
- **Generalization map:** Colored spectrum, nonstationarity, non-Gaussianity, spatial correlation, context dependence,
  leakage, and process memory are separate axes; this section covers only some.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The move beyond textbook channels is timely.

#### §18.11 — PSD definitions and examples

- **Wiener–Khinchin:** For a wide-sense stationary process, PSD is the Fourier transform of autocorrelation under stated
  one-/two-sided and `$2\pi$` conventions.
- **1/f sign:** Use `$1/|\omega|$` for a two-sided classical PSD and include infrared/ultraviolet cutoffs.
- **Lorentzian source:** Random telegraph noise from a single classical fluctuator gives a Lorentzian with amplitude and
  switching-rate factors; a coherently coupled resonant TLS can produce richer/split spectra.
- **White noise:** Infinite-band constant PSD has infinite total power and is an idealization; finite experimental
  bandwidth matters.
- **Filter connection:** Correctly ties spectral weight to sequence-dependent dephasing.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Three spectral shapes make an otherwise abstract diagnostic tangible.

#### §18.11 — noise spectroscopy

- **Delta-filter approximation:** CPMG filters have multiple finite-width harmonics; treating the principal peak at
  `$\omega\approx\pi N/T$` as a point sampler requires narrowband, weak-noise, Gaussian/dephasing assumptions.
- **Scanning protocol:** Varying `$N$` at fixed `$T$` changes pulse density and filter amplitude as well as peak
  frequency; pulse errors and finite pulse widths must be calibrated.
- **Reconstruction:** Extracting `$S(\omega)$` is an inverse problem, not direct point-by-point measurement in general.
  Report confidence, regularization, and accessible frequency window.
- **Strong “typical spectrum” claim:** The asserted 1 Hz–100 kHz band, TLS knee, and Johnson white floor require named
  devices/studies. Different qubit modalities, sweet spots, and couplings show different spectra.
- **Causal assignment:** A high-frequency white floor need not be Johnson noise specifically; amplifier/control phase
  noise, photon shot noise, and other mechanisms contribute.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Using the qubit as its own spectrum analyzer is an excellent practical idea.

#### §18.11 — CP-divisibility

- **Definition choice:** CP-divisibility is one standard quantum-Markovianity definition; say explicitly that other
  process-tensor and information-backflow notions are inequivalent.
- **Propagator dependence:** For noninvertible `$\mathcal E(t_1)$`, existence/definition of a CPTP intermediate map on
  the full state space has subtleties; a practitioner treatment can cite the formal definition.
- **Semigroup:** Time-homogeneous Lindblad semigroups are a correct special case.
- **Memory inference:** Failure of CP-divisibility signals non-Markovianity under this definition, but reduced dynamical
  maps alone do not completely characterize multi-time operational memory.
- **Gate-residue story:** A process tensor/conditional-environment picture is better for saying the effect of `$G_2$`
  depends on prior interventions; a one-parameter channel family cannot generally predict intervention histories.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Divisibility provides a clean algebraic test after the spectral intuition.

#### §18.11 — BLP trace-distance measure

- **Correct implication:** Any trace-distance revival for a state pair violates CP-divisibility because CPTP maps are
  contractive.
- **Converse fails:** CP-indivisible dynamics need not exhibit BLP backflow for the chosen/all state pairs; do not
  present the measure as equivalent to the preceding definition.
- **Optimization:** The BLP measure maximizes/integrates positive trace-distance derivative over pairs and times; a
  one-sentence formula would distinguish it from merely observing one revival.
- **Experimental burden:** State preparation/tomography/SPAM can mimic or hide small revivals.
- **Cross-reference:** Verify §12.6 states contractivity with the standard half trace norm convention.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Recovering distinguishability remains an unusually vivid measure of memory.

#### §18.11 — simulation implications

- **Markov insertion scope:** Independent post-gate Kraus channels model gate-local Markovian noise, but continuous-time
  noise during gates, simultaneous operations, gate dependence, and Lindblad evolution may require integrated channels.
- **“Cannot” overclaim:** Non-Markovian noise can be simulated by classical colored stochastic processes, hidden
  variables, process tensors, transfer tensors, pseudomodes, tensor networks, or enlarged baths. It is not limited to
  explicit unitary system–bath simulation.
- **Strong complexity defect:** Adding a “small bath” multiplies Hilbert-space dimension by the bath dimension; cost is
  polynomial only if the retained bath size/dimension grows logarithmically or remains constant. A faithful environment
  can require exponential memory or an unbounded continuum.
- **Initial correlations:** A joint system–bath state and intervention sequence must be specified; reduced Kraus maps
  may not compose.
- **Practical compromise:** Finite-memory kernels/process tensors can truncate correlations with an empirically tested
  memory length.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The history-dependent simulation problem is interesting, though the proposed workaround is
  falsely cheap.

#### §18.12 — tomography-versus-single-number framing

- **Parameter count:** A general `$d$`-dimensional channel has `$O(d^4)=O(16^n)$` real parameters before TP/CP
  constraints, while a Pauli-transfer matrix has `$4^n\times4^n$` entries. Saying process tomography returns “`~4^n`
  numbers” is a strong exponent error.
- **Cross-reference conflict:** §18.14 later correctly displays a `$4^n\times4^n$` matrix, making the opening internally
  inconsistent.
- **Single-number role:** Average fidelity can support monitoring/optimization but cannot certify fault tolerance,
  context dependence, leakage, or worst-case performance.
- **Terminology:** RB is standard for many gate platforms, while other modalities use decay, XEB, logical/cycle, or
  application benchmarks; avoid universalizing.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The compression from an exponential channel description to one decay is a strong setup.

#### §18.12 — Clifford RB protocol

- **Ordering:** The inversion is correct under the written operator convention; explicitly state rightmost gate acts
  first to avoid sequence-order confusion.
- **Noisy inverse:** `$C_{\rm inv}$` is itself compiled/noisy, and its error is folded into the averaged sequence rather
  than magically exact.
- **Sequence average:** Use multiple random sequences at each `$m$`, multiple shots per sequence, a range of lengths,
  randomized ordering/time interleaving, and uncertainty-aware fitting.
- **Survival:** For multiqubit RB, measuring only all-zero survival is standard, but leakage and erasures may require
  additional outcomes/models.
- **Fit validity:** `$A p^m+B$` follows approximately for gate-independent Markovian trace-preserving noise; gate
  dependence, leakage, drift, and non-Markovianity can produce multiexponential/nonexponential decay.
- **Conversion:** `$r=(d-1)(1-p)/d$` is correct for the depolarizing parameter convention; label it average infidelity
  per Clifford under assumptions, not generic physical error probability.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** The inverse-to-identity experiment is elegant and easy to remember.

#### §18.12 — why RB works

- **2-design:** The Clifford group is a unitary 2-design, sufficient to twirl a fixed channel to depolarizing form.
- **Gate-independent premise:** Real RB applies noisy Cliffords, so a literal single-channel group twirl is exact only
  under gate-independent/time-stationary assumptions; perturbative results extend beyond it.
- **SPAM robustness:** Constant SPAM enters `$A,B$` rather than `$p$` in the ideal model. Length-dependent drift,
  sequence-dependent measurement, leakage, and correlations can bias decay.
- **“Which Clifford fails”:** The group average intentionally does not localize gates; compilation weights primitives
  unevenly, so it is not an unweighted native-gate average.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The 2-design explanation gives the exponential fit real mathematical support.

#### §18.12 — limitations list

- **Average/localization:** Correct and important.
- **Coherence wording:** RB average fidelity does respond to coherent errors; it simply cannot infer their coherent
  character from the mean decay alone. “Sensitive only ... not coherent contributions” is false as written.
- **Assumptions:** Time-stationary gate-independent Markovian noise is the simplest analysis, but modern RB theory gives
  bounds/interpretations under weak gate dependence; “routinely violated” needs evidence.
- **Compilation:** Excellent warning. Report average native gates per Clifford, compiler, virtual-Z accounting, leakage,
  and simultaneous context.
- **Worst-case:** Diamond-distance bounds from RB infidelity can be loose; unitarity/purity metrics improve diagnosis but
  still require models.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** This compact list correctly prevents overreading the headline number apart from one wording
  error.

#### §18.12 — interleaved RB

- **Protocol ordering:** The final inversion must invert the ideal composite interleaved sequence, not just the random
  Cliffords; make this explicit.
- **Ratio:** A decay-parameter ratio estimates target-gate infidelity only under assumptions. Rigorous interleaved-RB
  results often provide bounds because reference-gate errors and target correlations do not factor exactly.
- **Gate dependence:** The paragraph appropriately notes correlations but understates how strongly they can invalidate a
  simple “specific error” interpretation.
- **Strong prevalence claim:** Individual two-qubit fidelities also come from XEB, cycle benchmarking, cross-entropy,
  process tomography, parity oscillations, Bell-state benchmarks, and direct RB. “Almost always” is false/unsourced.
- **SPAM/drift:** Reference and interleaved experiments should be interleaved in time to reduce drift bias.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The controlled comparison is intuitive and directly relevant to reported gate records.

#### §18.12 — direct, simultaneous, and mirror RB variants

- **Direct RB:** More than “native gates instead of Cliffords”; protocols sample native layers/germs from a gate set with
  an inversion/measurement scheme and specific theory. Cite the variant intended.
- **Simultaneous RB:** The rate difference measures context dependence under simultaneous schedules, which may include
  drift/heating/calibration changes—not a uniquely separable crosstalk component.
- **Mirror naming:** “Mirror randomized benchmarking” and “mirror circuit benchmarking” have related protocols; use
  exact names/citations consistently with §18.13.
- **Sensitivity claim:** Palindromic inverse structure can amplify or cancel coherent errors depending on randomized
  Pauli frames and construction. Do not assert universally greater coherence sensitivity without protocol detail.
- **Variant overload:** A small comparison table with inputs, fit, assumptions, output metric, and failure modes would be
  much easier to use.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The expanding toolkit is useful but acronym-dense.

#### §18.12 — XEB

- **Definition:** Linear XEB commonly averages `$D\,p_U(x)-1$` over samples; state the score, ensemble, and fidelity
  interpretation rather than describing only a vague decay.
- **Classical probabilities:** Ideal probabilities are required for sampled bitstrings in basic XEB, but batched
  amplitudes, tensor networks, patches, smaller calibration circuits, approximate proxies, and spoofing complicate the
  cost.
- **Strong threshold defect:** “Infeasible above ~50 qubits” is not a stable qubit-only boundary; depth, topology,
  fidelity, sample count, memory, and classical algorithm determine feasibility.
- **Logical non sequitur:** XEB’s classical verification burden is not “the reason XEB is itself a quantum-advantage
  demonstration.” XEB is a benchmark/statistic; an advantage claim additionally needs a hard circuit regime, quantum
  samples, matched fidelity, and best-classical comparison.
- **Fidelity assumptions:** Relating XEB score to circuit fidelity assumes chaotic/Porter–Thomas-like circuits and a
  suitable noise model; coherent/model-specific noise and spoofing can break interpretation.
- **2019 role:** Correctly important to Sycamore, but cite the precise protocol and separate calibration XEB from the
  sampling experiment.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** A benchmark whose verification approaches the target hardness is fascinating, if not itself
  proof of advantage.

#### §18.13 — isolation-versus-simultaneity framing

- **Reality check:** Concurrent operation and context dependence are central system-level concerns.
- **RB premise:** Single-qubit RB may itself use parallel Cliffords; standard isolated RB is not inherently sequential
  across the whole chip. Phrase as a comparison between isolated and scheduled simultaneous contexts.
- **Clock cycle:** Hardware gates have unequal durations and overlapping pulses; a “same clock cycle” layer requires a
  scheduler definition.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** It shifts attention from component specifications to system behavior effectively.

#### §18.13 — simultaneous RB

- **Protocol:** Running independent RB sequences in parallel is standard, but inversion/sampling, neighbor sets, drive
  frequencies, and scheduling should be specified.
- **Attribution:** The difference from isolated decay is a context-dependent simultaneous penalty, not uniquely a
  “crosstalk contribution”; calibration drift, heating, shared control constraints, and fit changes can contribute.
- **Strong current-number claim:** The 1.5×–3× range needs a defined platform dataset, time, qubit selection, confidence,
  and baseline. It cannot describe “current devices” generally.
- **Ratio instability:** A multiplicative ratio can look huge when isolated error is tiny; absolute added infidelity and
  spatial map are more informative.
- **QEC relevance:** Simultaneous Clifford context may differ from the repeated stabilizer-measurement schedule.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The isolation penalty is intuitively important and easy to visualize on a coupling map.

#### §18.13 — cycle benchmarking

- **Cycle definition:** A cycle is a specified parallel layer with durations/idles, not necessarily one universal clock
  tick or a mathematically maximal layer.
- **Protocol precision:** Cycle benchmarking uses randomized Pauli dressing and character benchmarking ideas to estimate
  process/Pauli fidelities under assumptions; cite the exact construction.
- **Strong isolation claim:** Twirling makes the averaged effective cycle channel Pauli-diagonal but does not magically
  separate all individual Pauli error rates from SPAM, correlations, leakage, or finite statistics.
- **QEC connection:** Whole stabilizer cycles/cycle error models are indeed more relevant than isolated gate averages,
  though logical performance still depends on space-time correlations and decoder.
- **Average preservation:** Randomized compiling changes coherent structure at the ensemble level and must be included
  consistently in the implemented cycle.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Treating the scheduled layer as the primitive is an excellent system-engineering insight.

#### §18.13 — mirror circuit benchmarking

- **Protocol:** `$U$` followed by its ideal inverse has a known output, enabling scalable tests without classically
  simulating every amplitude; randomization details and native-gate compilation determine what is measured.
- **Coherent-error claim:** Mirror structure may cancel identical coherent errors when inverse gates reverse them or
  amplify other errors; randomized Pauli dressing is essential. Say it samples sequencing/context sensitivity rather
  than simply “includes” coherence unlike RB.
- **Name consistency:** Earlier §18.12 says “Mirror RB”; decide whether the source protocol is mirror RB, mirror circuit
  benchmarking, or randomized mirror circuits.
- **Forecasting:** Correlation with arbitrary application failure is empirical and workload-dependent. Benchmark circuits
  may not match algorithm structure.
- **Publication prevalence:** “Now reported ... in many publications” is current and needs examples.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Run-and-unrun is a satisfying, scalable diagnostic idea.

#### §18.13 — purity benchmarking

- **Protocol defect/suspicion:** Purity benchmarking estimates unitarity using purity-sensitive/second-moment data from
  randomized sequences; calling it simply the “second-moment statistics of survival probability” may be inaccurate for
  the intended protocol. Give the measured observables and estimator.
- **Incoherent component:** Unitarity quantifies how much noise preserves traceless-operator norm and bounds incoherence;
  the purity decay is not a universal direct rate equal to “the incoherent part.”
- **Comparison:** RB infidelity plus unitarity can bound coherent versus stochastic character, not necessarily uniquely
  isolate a ratio for arbitrary nonunital/leakage/gate-dependent noise.
- **Qualitative result:** Coherent-dominated error can show high unitarity/slower purity loss relative to RB decay;
  “much smaller” requires a model and normalization.
- **SPAM:** Purity benchmarking has robustness properties but still needs multi-axis measurements and fit assumptions.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Using purity to expose harmless-looking coherent error is conceptually strong.

#### §18.14 — QPT setup and scaling

- **PTM dimensions:** A channel on `$n$` qubits has a `$4^n\times4^n$` Pauli-transfer matrix, correctly stated here and
  contradicting §18.12’s “`~4^n` numbers.”
- **Input basis wording:** One needs `$d^2=4^n$` linearly independent physical input states; the Pauli operator basis
  itself contains non-density operators that cannot all be “prepared.” Distinguish operator basis from state set.
- **Measurement settings:** Full output state tomography requires an informationally complete POVM/settings and many
  shots; linear inversion is not necessarily overdetermined unless extra settings are chosen.
- **Shot-complexity claim:** `$\Theta(16^n/\epsilon^2)$` depends on error norm, confidence, estimator, physicality
  constraints, and allocation across parameters; source or soften it.
- **Strong feasibility rhetoric:** Two-qubit QPT is routinely feasible though costly; three-plus scales badly, but
  “impossible above three” is not a theorem and depends on sparsity/structure/resources.
- **SPAM:** Correctly identifies systematic bias; preparation and measurement maps compose with the target so naive QPT
  cannot identify them separately.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The exponential wall is clear, though the precise experiment count needs care.

#### §18.14 — GST premise and identifiability

- **Strong “resolves” defect:** GST handles SPAM self-consistently but cannot uniquely identify a gate set because
  operational probabilities are invariant under gauge transformations. It does not fully resolve physical attribution.
- **Unknown set:** GST estimates a chosen gate-set/model family plus preparations/measurements from circuits; model
  completeness and Markovian/time-stationary assumptions are load-bearing.
- **Germs:** Germs are short sequences repeated to amplify identifiable error parameters, combined with fiducials and
  sequence lengths. Define all three rather than “germ set of repeated short circuits.”
- **Gauge fixing:** A gauge optimization chooses a representative, often near targets; it is not data-derived unique
  truth.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Joint self-calibration is an elegant answer to QPT’s circularity, even with gauge limits.

#### §18.14 — GST output list

- **PTMs/state/POVMs:** These are gauge-dependent representations whose jointly predicted probabilities are the
  operational invariant.
- **Metric caution:** Average/process fidelity and especially diamond distance to an ideal target can change under gauge
  choice unless comparisons and gauge optimization are carefully defined.
- **Uncertainty:** Include confidence regions/error bars; a point-estimate matrix with millions of shots is not enough.
- **Goodness of fit:** Likelihood-based model violation can flag statistically significant mismatch but does not identify
  non-Markovianity uniquely; drift, leakage, context dependence, bad likelihood/noise model, or experimental bugs can
  also cause it.
- **“Formal” statistic:** Name the statistic/degrees of freedom and account for multiple testing/large-data sensitivity.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** A full device model plus an alarm for model failure is an attractive promise that needs
  epistemic restraint.

#### §18.14 — GST strengths and costs

- **Consistency:** GST is self-consistent within its modeled gate set and Markovian assumptions; “fully consistent
  description of the device” overstates extrapolation to untested contexts/times.
- **Failure detection:** Goodness-of-fit rejects a model but cannot certify which assumption failed.
- **Cost units:** `$10^5$–`$10^6$` “circuit executions” may mean shots, total samples, or distinct circuits; define gate
  set, maximum length, confidence, and implementation.
- **Two-qubit feasibility:** Costs grow with parameters and long germs; modern reduced/model-based GST variants differ.
- **Daily-calibration claim:** Full 50-qubit GST is infeasible, but local/tiled/reduced GST or rapid diagnostics may run
  routinely. “Cannot” should refer to global full GST under stated resources.
- **Post-processing:** Optimization can be nonconvex/expensive and gauge/physicality handling matters; good to mention.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The rigor-versus-cost tradeoff is compelling and realistic.

#### §18.14 — benchmark selection guide

- **Strong practical value:** Choosing the cheapest diagnostic that answers the actual question is exactly the right
  operational principle.
- **RB:** Good for stable aggregate monitoring, subject to drift/gate-dependence and compilation.
- **Interleaved RB:** Estimates/bounds a target gate only against a reference model; not automatically a bottleneck
  locator.
- **Simultaneous/cycle:** Context/cycle performance, not pure causal crosstalk isolation.
- **Mirror:** Useful scalable circuit-layer benchmark; “forecasting” must be workload-validated.
- **Purity:** Estimates unitarity/incoherence under assumptions, not a unique coherent ratio.
- **QPT:** Even with independently “well-characterized” SPAM, residual calibration bias persists.
- **GST:** Best suited to small modeled gate sets for detailed diagnosis, with gauge/non-Markovian caveats.
- **Hierarchy limitation:** These tools are not strictly nested in information/cost and answer different questions; a
  decision tree is more accurate than one cheap-to-expensive line.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** This is the most directly reusable paragraph in the chapter.

#### §18.15 — simulator-model framing

- **Definition:** Inserting channels/stochastic faults around ideal operations is the standard circuit-level approach,
  but pulse-level Lindblad, Hamiltonian, trajectory, tensor-network, and process-tensor simulations are also noise
  models.
- **Prediction target:** A model must specify whether it predicts bitstring distributions, expectation values,
  logical-error rates, leakage, calibration observables, or qualitative trends; no one notion of “what a device will
  produce” exists.
- **Three layers:** These are three useful levels, not an industry-standard exhaustive hierarchy. Correlated Pauli,
  coherent-unitary, erasure/loss, Lindblad/pulse, and learned models fall between/outside them.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The fidelity ladder is a practical way into model selection.

#### §18.15 — depolarizing-only model

- **RB conversion defect:** The depolarizing parameter `$p$` is not generally equal to measured RB average error; use
  the dimension-dependent relation established in §18.12 and distinguish error per Clifford from per native gate.
- **“Faithful” misuse:** A depolarizing fit is deliberately phenomenological and may match one average number; calling
  it the “crudest faithful model” overstates physical fidelity.
- **Isotropy:** Correct for full depolarization, though a one-qubit depolarizing channel’s convention (`$p$` total Pauli
  probability versus shrinkage probability) must be fixed.
- **Memorylessness:** Independent insertion imposes Markovian, gate-local, stationary noise, as stated.
- **SPAM-free:** Only if preparation/measurement channels are deliberately omitted; “depolarizing-only” describes that
  modeling choice.
- **Success prediction:** Average circuit success can deviate badly under coherent, biased, nonunital, leakage, and
  observable-specific errors even at matched RB infidelity. “Works well” needs a circuit/noise study.
- **SDK-default claim:** Time-sensitive and configuration-dependent; verify Qiskit/Cirq/PennyLane/default simulator
  behavior. Most simulators are noiseless unless a noise model is supplied.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** A deliberately crude baseline is valuable when its failure envelope is explicit.

#### §18.15 — Pauli-channel model

- **Single-qubit scope:** `$p_X,p_Y,p_Z$` describes one qubit. A multiqubit gate has `$4^k-1$` nonidentity Pauli faults,
  including correlated terms, not just three probabilities.
- **Cycle-benchmarking overclaim:** Cycle benchmarking estimates Pauli fidelities/eigenvalues under twirling and model
  assumptions; reconstructing all Pauli error probabilities requires transforms, sufficient experiments, and can face
  sampling/SPAM/leakage issues. It does not simply return three probabilities directly.
- **Stochastic simulation:** Sampling a Pauli fault avoids density-matrix branching, but propagating the quantum state
  remains exponential for general non-Clifford circuits. It is efficient with stabilizer structure or specialized
  trajectory/tensor methods, not generically.
- **“Exponentially cheaper”:** A state-vector trajectory uses `$O(2^n)$` memory versus `$O(4^n)$` density-matrix memory,
  an exponential ratio in `$n$`, but many trajectories are required for sampling error. State the comparison.
- **Pauli frame:** For Clifford circuits, faults propagate efficiently as Paulis; through non-Clifford gates they do not
  remain a simple classical Pauli frame without additional simulation machinery.
- **Usage prevalence:** “Most large-scale” is broad and should be sourced/scoped to stabilizer/QEC simulations.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Bias-resolved Pauli rates are a useful intermediate model, though the simulation claim is too
  cheap.

#### §18.15 — realistic-device model

- **Additivity/composition:** Combining separately measured channels assumes a composition order and independence;
  `$T_1/T_2$`, RB error, crosstalk, and leakage measurements may already overlap, causing double counting.
- **Full Kraus scaling:** Arbitrary multiqubit Kraus channels are exponentially costly; “realistic” must still be
  locality-/structure-limited.
- **Crosstalk matrix:** Static linear drive transfer does not represent ZZ, spectator-state, measurement, nonlinear, or
  history-dependent crosstalk.
- **Leakage:** Requires enlarged Hilbert dimension or erasure/hidden-state model; ordinary qubit Kraus simulators may not
  support it seamlessly.
- **SDK audit:** Qiskit Aer, Cirq, Stim, and PennyLane Lightning expose different capabilities. Stim is specialized for
  stabilizer/Pauli/measurement-error models; verify whether Lightning supports every stated feature and current APIs.
- **Strong bottleneck claim:** Calibration/model identifiability is important, but exact simulation cost, correlated-
  model representation, software limitations, and model validation can be equal/larger bottlenecks.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The component assembly feels actionable while risking a false sense of physical realism.

#### §18.15 — model fidelity and unexplained factor-of-two rule

- **Useful honesty:** Quantitative device prediction is genuinely difficult and qualitative/order-of-magnitude models
  are more common.
- **Metric:** “Output distributions” need total-variation/XEB/KL/observable error and shot uncertainty; “order of
  magnitude” is undefined for a distribution.
- **Failure modes incomplete:** Calibration drift, coherent control error, gate/context dependence, spatial
  correlations, measurement backaction, incorrect pulse scheduling, parameter covariance, and SPAM also cause model
  failure.
- **Unsupported diagnostic heuristic:** A `~2×` disagreement has no universal statistical meaning, and attributing it
  “usually” to temporal correlation, leakage, or memory requires a dataset. Model error could be mundane.
- **Validation:** Use held-out circuits across depths/structures/times, predictive intervals, and residual diagnostics
  rather than a fixed factor threshold.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The simulator-versus-hardware gap is important, but the twofold rule creates spurious
  certainty.

#### §18.15 — Stim and stabilizer noise

- **Scope:** Stabilizer-code syndrome-extraction circuits are largely Clifford plus Pauli preparation/measurement/reset,
  making Stim extremely effective; not every QEC component (magic-state injection, non-Clifford logical operations,
  analog leakage) is Clifford.
- **Performance unit:** “Million-qubit-second-scale” is ambiguous—simulated qubits times physical seconds, detector
  samples per CPU second, or circuit spacetime volume? Quote a reproducible benchmark/version/hardware.
- **Mechanism:** Stim uses stabilizer/tableau and detector-error-model techniques with Pauli noise; “tracking Pauli
  frames stochastically” is only part of its operation.
- **Threshold studies:** It is a major tool, not the unique workhorse; decoders and correlated/leakage models may require
  other simulators.
- **Cross-reference:** Verify §19.12 demonstrates or cites Stim rather than merely mentioning thresholds.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** A concrete high-performance tool grounds the modeling discussion.

#### §18.16 — error-budget premise

- **Exactness:** Even a fully specified noise model may only predict probabilities numerically/approximately; an exact
  answer also depends on input, observable/success criterion, compilation, and time-varying calibration.
- **Attribution versus prediction:** An error budget can prioritize components but average component infidelities do not
  uniquely attribute an observed application failure.
- **Metric:** Define “success probability” per algorithm; fidelity, heavy-output score, expectation bias, and all-zero
  survival differ.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Translating calibration data into a circuit budget is precisely the practitioner task.

#### §18.16 — additive approximation and formula

- **Indexing defect:** The formula sums over operations `$i$` and then multiplies `$\epsilon_i^{1q}$` by a count
  `$n_i^{1q}$`, apparently counting twice. Use category sums:
  `$N_{1q}r_{1q}+N_{2q}r_{2q}+\sum_j t_j/T_j+\cdots$`.
- **Metric compatibility:** Average infidelities, assignment probabilities, leakage rates, and crosstalk excess are not
  the same event probability and cannot generally be added.
- **Independence:** Linear first-order expansion requires small, roughly independent stochastic faults and an observable/
  failure model. `$r_{\rm total}\ll1$` is necessary but not sufficient.
- **SPAM count:** Preparation/readout occurs per qubit/measurement/reset, potentially many times per shot, not one
  scalar “added once for each shot.”
- **Parallel operations:** Counts ignore duration/parallelism/context; simultaneous gates may not contribute
  independently.
- **Higher order:** For independent Bernoulli failure, exact survival is `$\prod_i(1-p_i)$`; the sum is its first-order
  union approximation. Showing this would clarify scope.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The spreadsheet idea is useful, but the displayed expression itself needs reconstruction.

#### §18.16 — component-attribution table

- **Gate labels:** RB gives errors per Clifford unless converted to native operations; a circuit count may count native
  gates, producing a unit mismatch.
- **Idle:** Multiply a rate/channel-derived infidelity by scheduled duration, not “idle time” under a universal scalar;
  relaxation and dephasing coefficients differ.
- **Readout:** Correlated assignment and measurement-induced transitions prevent simple rate times count at scale.
- **Crosstalk double counting:** The simultaneous-minus-isolated gap already includes extra gate/context error; adding it
  alongside simultaneous gate rates can double count.
- **Leakage persistence:** Leakage is not a one-gate independent failure; one event affects many subsequent cycles and
  LRU cadence.
- **Vendor-history claim:** “Became common” is historical and should cite representative reports.
- **Factor-of-two rule:** A good budget should come with statistical/model uncertainty, not a universal factor-two
  reconciliation target.
- **Residual attribution:** When it fails, coherent calibration, drift, metric conversion, compilation, SPAM,
  correlations, or wrong success model may be responsible—not usually only memory/leakage.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The table would be genuinely practical if its rows were nonoverlapping and dimensionally
  consistent.

#### §18.16 — coherent/correlated limits

- **Coherent law:** `$n^2\epsilon$` is a small-angle worst/aligned-circuit regime, not a universal compounding rule; it
  saturates/oscillates and ideal gates rotate error axes.
- **Correlations:** Positive statistical correlation of fault indicators does not automatically make expected total
  error larger than the sum of marginals; it changes joint/failure structure. Circuit-level constructive interference
  needs a model.
- **Anti-correlation:** Not necessarily rare, especially under echo, composite pulses, alternating calibrations, or
  conservation constraints; “rare but real” is unsupported.
- **TLS example:** Random-telegraph TLS drift alternates states/sign over switching events, but this is not synonymous
  with deliberately anticorrelated per-gate cancellation.
- **Better bound:** Present the additive budget as a first-order baseline and compare coherent worst-case/Pauli
  stochastic simulations rather than asserting scalar corrections.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The warning is necessary, though its probability language is loose.

#### §18.16 — fidelity/error conversion

- **Definition dependence:** If `$F$` is explicitly average gate fidelity, average infidelity is `$r=1-F_{\rm avg}$` by
  definition. “Gate fidelity” might instead mean process/entanglement fidelity, state fidelity, or RB-derived EPC.
- **RB:** RB fits `$p$`; conversion to average infidelity uses `$(d-1)(1-p)/d` under assumptions. It does not return
  `$\epsilon$` directly and then need an optional factor.
- **Pauli error:** For a Pauli channel, total nonidentity probability relates to average infidelity by a dimension
  factor; it is not identical.
- **Diamond convention:** Specify full diamond norm versus half diamond distance. It is not merely “a different bound”
  but a worst-case channel metric with inequalities relative to average fidelity.
- **PTM:** Process tomography estimates a channel representation from which multiple fidelity metrics can be computed,
  subject to SPAM/statistical/physicality bias.
- **Positive:** The warning not to mix these numbers is excellent and should be accompanied by a conversion table.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** This is indispensable metric hygiene.

#### §18.17 — workflow framing

- **Grammar:** “From designed to ran successfully” should be “from design to a successful hardware run” or “from
  designed to run successfully.”
- **Universality:** This resembles a superconducting calibration-lab workflow, not the standard path for every user,
  vendor cloud, photonic experiment, trapped-ion system, or logical-QEC project.
- **Iterative nature:** Calibration/model/compile/run/validate loops overlap; a diagram with feedback arrows would help.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** A concrete workflow is a welcome payoff after the metric catalogue.

#### §18.17 — daily calibration

- **Scale:** RB/interleaved RB on every qubit/coupler plus readout and T1/T2 sweeps can be enormous on large devices;
  labs use subsets, automated calibration graphs, drift triggers, parallelization, and targeted checks.
- **Time claim:** “Minutes to tens of minutes” is hardware-, shot-, queue-, qubit-count-, and protocol-dependent; cite a
  particular system.
- **Two-qubit IRB:** Full IRB for every coupler daily may be too expensive and is not universal practice.
- **Queue gate:** Cloud/vendor operations and continuous calibration schedules differ; avoid presenting one lab’s day.
- **Drift:** Calibration itself takes time during which early parameters may change.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The notion that each experimental day begins with metrology conveys the operational reality.

#### §18.17 — per-experiment characterization

- **Targeting:** Measuring specific cycles/contexts is good practice.
- **Cost:** Full cycle/purity/simultaneous RB can consume substantial shots and may perturb the time window of the actual
  experiment; use sentinel circuits/interleaving.
- **Purity criterion:** Unitarity diagnosis may matter even when not explicitly requested because coherent error affects
  extrapolation; “if” is a resource choice.
- **Model mismatch:** Benchmark circuits should match gates, qubits, schedule, depth, and calibration epoch.
- **Entertainment: 3/5.** Sensible and concise.

#### §18.17 — model/compiler step

- **False either/or:** Configuring a simulator and noise-aware compilation are complementary, not alternatives.
- **Calibration conversion:** RB/T1/T2/readout data do not uniquely determine a channel model; document inference
  assumptions and uncertainty.
- **Compiler objectives:** Minimize weighted error, crosstalk, leakage, routing, duration, and measurement latency, not
  only idle time/bad couplers.
- **Dynamic data:** Mapping/scheduling based on stale calibration can hurt; timestamp and robust optimization matter.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Closing the loop from measurement to compilation is practically satisfying.

#### §18.17 — compile-time mitigation

- **Category blur:** Pulse shaping is calibration/control design; dynamical decoupling and randomized compiling are
  circuit transformations; mid-circuit measurement is an algorithm/control primitive. Calling all compile-time
  “mitigation” hides distinct guarantees.
- **Twirling timing:** Randomized compilation creates an ensemble of physical circuits executed at run time, even if
  generated at compile time.
- **DD tradeoff:** Added pulses can introduce error/crosstalk and interfere with gates; schedule constraints matter.
- **Mid-circuit claim:** Measurement reduces error only in specific reset, feed-forward, erasure-conversion, or
  verification protocols and can add latency/backaction.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The menu is useful but taxonomically loose.

#### §18.17 — runtime/post-processing and validation

- **List mismatch:** Virtual distillation requires extra quantum copies/entangling circuits at run time plus classical
  post-processing; ZNE/PEC also require circuit ensembles, not merely post-processing.
- **Validation target:** On classically hard circuits the ideal output is unavailable, so validation needs held-out
  observables, scalable witnesses, cross-device checks, logical syndromes, or small/structured instances.
- **Shot noise:** Agreement “within shot noise” ignores model-parameter uncertainty, drift, multiple comparisons, and
  approximation bias.
- **Iteration risk:** Tuning mitigation on validation outputs can overfit; hold out circuits/observables.
