#### §34.1 — linear-systems opening

- **False statement:** Not “every postulate” is a linear operator acting on a vector. Measurement probabilities are
  quadratic in amplitudes; normalized state-update conditioned on an outcome is nonlinear; mixed-state dynamics uses
  linear completely positive maps on density operators.
- **State scope:** Pure \(n\)-qubit states are unit vectors in \(\mathbb C^{2^n}\); general states are density matrices.
- **Gate scope:** An \(n\)-qubit global unitary lies in \(U(2^n)\), but a local gate is embedded as a tensor-product/
  sparse operator; most circuit gates are not stored as full matrices.
- **Composition:** State-vector column convention gives later gates left-multiplying earlier products; state this
  convention.
- **Invariant:** Unitary evolution preserves all inner products, not only norm, and isolated closed-system dynamics also
  preserves purity/entropy spectrum.
- **Kalman analogy:** Kalman filters include affine evolution, stochastic noise, covariance update and Bayesian
  conditioning, so “otherwise same” is too strong.
- **Anti-spooky tone:** Good, but replacing mystery with inaccurate linearity is counterproductive.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Immediate familiarity.

#### §34.1 — classical simulator versus quantum cost

- **Variable collision:** Classical “\(n\)-dimensional” state followed by \(n\) qubits uses \(n\) for different
  dimensions; rename classical dimension \(d\).
- **Classical update:** Dense matrix-vector multiply costs \(O(d^2)\), but structured/sparse state-space models can be
  \(O(d)\) or better; storage is \(O(d)\).
- **Simulator gate cost wrong:** Applying a one- or two-qubit gate to an \(n\)-qubit dense state vector is
  \(O(2^n)\), yes; a general \(n\)-qubit dense gate would cost \(O(4^n)\). State/locality matters.
- **Density simulator:** Storage is \(O(4^n)\), while applying a local channel/gate is also \(O(4^n)\) up to constants;
  a dense superoperator would be worse.
- **Major false claim:** A quantum computer does not pay \(O(1)\) to update an arbitrary \(2^n\)-amplitude state. A
  fixed-locality physical gate may take constant primitive time, while useful global transformations require circuits
  whose gate count/depth scale with \(n\), connectivity, precision and error correction.
- **“Stores vector”:** The state has exponentially many amplitudes but they are not individually addressable classical
  storage. The quotation marks help, yet “implicit storage is entire engineering point” encourages the database fallacy.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** The cost contrast is central but currently dangerously overstated.

#### §34.1 — claimed opportunity examples/output caveat

- **Vector-length fallacy:** A classical bottleneck on a \(2^n\)-length vector is not sufficient evidence a quantum
  algorithm helps. Efficient state preparation, succinct operator implementation, interference structure and compact
  output are all required.
- **QFT comparison:** Quantum QFT operates on amplitudes of a prepared quantum state and samples/uses the transformed
  state; classical FFT outputs all coefficients. They solve different I/O tasks.
- **Graph walks:** A graph of \(2^n\) vertices must have succinct neighbor/oracle access implementable efficiently.
- **“Evaluate every input”:** Quantum superposition evaluates an oracle coherently, but measurement does not reveal all
  values; only global properties accessible through interference can help.
- **Output caveat:** Excellent and should be moved before examples so it constrains, rather than repairs, the intuition.
- **Part reference:** Verify algorithms are Part 6.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** This is the key conceptual tension.

#### §34.1 — nonlinear-gate paragraph

- **Physical law:** Standard closed-system quantum dynamics is linear/unitary, while normalized conditional measurement,
  effective mean-field equations and nonlinear open feedback require careful distinctions; “nonlinear gate” should mean
  deterministic nonlinear evolution of pure states.
- **Second-law analogy:** Both are physical principles, but one is dynamical structure and one thermodynamic/statistical;
  avoid implying identical epistemic status.
- **Signaling/cloning/complexity:** Deterministic nonlinear quantum mechanics can enable superluminal signaling and
  dramatically alter complexity, but exact consequences depend on the nonlinear model.
- **NP claim:** Abrams–Lloyd-type nonlinear quantum mechanics can solve NP-complete and #P problems efficiently under
  particular nonlinearities/precision assumptions; cite rather than universalize any distinguishability primitive.
- **Ambiguous sentence:** “Distinguish superposition from linear superposition of outputs” needs a formal map:
  \(G(\alpha\psi+\beta\phi)\ne\alpha G(\psi)+\beta G(\phi)\).
- **Price metaphor:** The large Hilbert space does not arise as a “price” paid for linearity; linearity and tensor-product
  composition jointly define the model.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Forbidden nonlinear computing is fascinating.

#### §34.2 — Hadamard/Walsh analogy

- **Transform:** \(H^{\otimes n}\) is the normalized Walsh–Hadamard transform; correct.
- **Basis-state input:** It maps \(|y\rangle\) to
  \(2^{-n/2}\sum_x(-1)^{x\cdot y}|x\rangle\), not a generic “expansion” requiring computation output.
- **Parity basis:** Walsh characters encode bitwise parity; “frequency basis” is analogy, not a physical Fourier
  frequency.
- **Arbitrary input omitted:** The transform acts on amplitudes of arbitrary superpositions too.
- **DSP claim:** Walsh–Hadamard transforms occur in coding/signal processing, but “every apply H means switch to
  parity/frequency basis” fails for a single Hadamard used in gate synthesis, state creation, interference or basis
  measurement.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Strong when scoped to registers.

#### §34.2 — QFT/DFT analogy and complexity

- **Transform identity:** QFT is the normalized DFT over \(\mathbb Z_{2^n}\) on amplitude indices; correct.
- **Depth/gates:** Standard exact approximate circuit has \(O(n^2)\) two-qubit gates and naïve depth \(O(n^2)\), but
  parallel scheduling/connectivity/approximation can reduce depth. Avoid equating gate count with depth.
- **False classical comparison:** Classical FFT on \(N=2^n\) values costs \(O(N\log N)=O(n2^n)\), but it reads/writes
  all \(N\) coefficients; QFT neither accepts a freely accessible classical array in poly(\(n\)) time nor outputs all
  transformed values. State the input/output mismatch prominently.
- **Algorithm summary:** Phase estimation/order finding use interference/QFT sampling, broadly correct; Shor also needs
  modular exponentiation and classical postprocessing.
- **Windowing/leakage:** Finite phase-register resolution produces Dirichlet-kernel leakage; window-state engineering
  can change tails. Analogy is useful but not all standard DSP intuitions transfer automatically.
- **Cross-reference:** Verify Chapter 14 explicit discussion.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** One of the best bridges after cost correction.

#### §34.2 — Hamiltonian evolution/filtering

- **Diagonal action:** Correct spectral phase evolution.
- **“Bandpass filtering” incorrect:** Unitary phase evolution preserves eigencomponent magnitudes; it does not attenuate
  stop bands like a bandpass filter. Phase estimation/QSP/postselection can implement spectral filters, but bare
  \(e^{-iHt}\) is phase modulation.
- **Choosing time:** Sets accumulated eigenphases/resolution/aliasing, not by itself a frequency-domain filter response.
- **False Trotter analogy:** Product-formula Trotterization approximates noncommuting operator exponentials; it is not
  “the same finite-difference approximation” as discretizing a continuous DSP filter. Both discretize evolution in some
  contexts, but the numerical error mechanism is commutators, not finite differences.
- **QSP:** Correctly described as polynomial transformation of singular/eigenvalues under block-encoding/signal-unitary
  conditions; cite section content.
- **Filter design:** Strong analogy specifically for QSP/QSVT.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Very attractive analogy with two serious category errors.

#### §34.2 — readout break

- **Strong caveat:** Correctly distinguishes circuit design from output access.
- **Classical readout:** Entire transformed signal takes \(O(2^n)\), not merely “linear time” without naming signal
  length.
- **Quantum sampling:** A shot samples a measurement distribution in a chosen basis; it does not directly sample complex
  amplitudes/phases.
- **Other extraction:** Amplitude estimation, tomography, shadows and expectation estimation provide different partial
  access with their own costs.
- **Recommendation:** Move this warning earlier and repeat it adjacent to QFT complexity.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Critical reality check.

#### §34.3 — quantum-register analogy

- **“Stores a superposition”:** Standard shorthand, but amplitudes are not independently readable stored values.
- **Wrong mental model:** A coherent quantum state is not “a probability distribution you can compute on coherently.”
  Probabilities lack phase; amplitudes are complex quasiprobability-like data whose interference is essential. This
  analogy would collapse BQP toward stochastic computation.
- **Better model:** A normalized complex amplitude vector evolving reversibly, from which a distribution emerges only
  after choosing a measurement.
- **Normalization degrees:** \(2^n\) complex amplitudes have normalization plus global-phase redundancy; “one
  normalization equation” omits unobservable global phase.
- **Parallel universe:** Correct to reject as literal explanation, but §34.8 must do so.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Accessible sentence teaches a damaging simplification.

#### §34.3 — ancilla/scratch/RAII analogy

- **Discarding:** Tracing out a nonzero ancilla is not the same as measuring it with a recorded outcome, though both can
  decohere a system entangled with it. If the ancilla is separable—even in a non-\(|0\rangle\) state—it can be safely
  discarded without affecting the live system.
- **Uncomputation condition:** Return work ancillas to a fixed product state (often \(|0\rangle\)); uncomputing may erase
  desired output if it has not been copied coherently/used via phase kickback.
- **Irreversibility:** Reset can release entropy/require environment; fault-tolerant workflows measure/reset ancillas
  routinely.
- **RAII mismatch:** RAII guarantees cleanup on scope exit; quantum uncomputation is explicit reversible computation and
  cannot always be automatically synthesized cheaply.
- **“Leaks advantage”:** Memorable and directionally useful.
- **Cross-references:** Verify §§9.3–9.4.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Excellent analogy with a precise separability caveat needed.

#### §34.3 — no-cloning/ownership analogy

- **Theorem:** Correct standard map impossibility for arbitrary unknown states; replace any malformed escapes if present.
- **Move-only analogy:** Helpful for linear-type discipline, but quantum information can be delocalized/entangled and
  teleportation transfers state while consuming entanglement/classical messages.
- **Ownership:** Qubits do not have one physical “owner” in entangled systems; wires label subsystems, while logical
  information can be encoded nonlocally.
- **Classical source exception:** Known computational-basis states can be re-prepared/copy-basis CNOT; an unknown state
  promised to be from an orthogonal basis set can also be cloned in that basis. “Unless source is classical” needs this
  exact meaning.
- **C++/Rust:** Very effective for software readers.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** One of the chapter’s strongest analogies.

#### §34.3 — measurement/syscall analogy

- **“Only non-unitary”:** False in realistic/extended circuit models: reset, noise channels, state preparation,
  discarding, classically controlled channels and postselection are nonunitary. In the ideal pure-state postulates,
  measurement is the designated nonunitary primitive.
- **“Non-functional”:** Functional programming can model random/state effects; use “nondeterministic and state-changing”
  rather than misuse functional.
- **Collapse:** Interpretation-dependent language; operationally the conditional state updates and unconditioned state is
  dephased by measurement channel.
- **Cost generalization false:** Measurement is not always the slowest operation and is not “the source of most
  decoherence.” Superconducting readout can be slow relative to gates; ion measurement can be much slower; photonic
  computation is measurement-native; decoherence mostly arises during storage/gates/environmental coupling.
- **Syscall choice:** `read()` is closer than `write()` because measurement extracts a classical outcome; both cross a
  boundary.
- **“Cross as little”:** Mid-circuit measurement/reset/feed-forward can reduce depth/ancillas and enable QEC/MBQC; fewer
  measurements is not universal advice.
- **Batching:** Hardware shots/circuits often batch, but measurement outcomes may be needed adaptively.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Highly memorable, dangerously universal as advice.

#### §34.3 — shot-cost comparison

- **Sampling algorithms:** Expectation estimation/VQE-like workloads require repeated shots, but Chapter 26 scope should
  be verified.
- **One-shot algorithms:** Shor/Grover/phase estimation still have bounded failure probabilities and need repetitions,
  verification and classical postprocessing; not literally one measurement always yields the answer.
- **Amortization metaphor:** Constructive interference concentrates probability, but circuit cost is paid each run; it
  does not amortize a syscall across a circuit in the conventional performance sense.
- **Information metric:** Maximum useful information per state preparation/circuit execution is the right optimization
  idea; mention Fisher information/variance.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Strong systems intuition after qualification.

#### Chapter 34 partial-pass checkpoint after §34.3

- **Coverage added:** Status/navigation, both opening/roadmap units, and every equation/analogy in §§34.1–34.3 have
  separate fine-grained notes.
- **Strongest issues:** “Every postulate is linear” ignores conditional measurement; fixed local quantum gates are
  misleadingly assigned \(O(1)\) total update cost; Hamiltonian evolution is called bandpass filtering; Trotterization
  is equated with finite differences; a quantum state is called a probability distribution, erasing phase; discarding
  is equated with measurement regardless of separability; measurement is called the only nonunitary operation and source
  of most decoherence; and the reading guide does not match visible section contents.
- **Status:** Second pass remains in progress for this manuscript file; resume at §34.4.

#### §34.4 — gates/instructions/unity paragraph

- **Instruction analogy:** Useful, but physical gates, virtual frame changes, measurements, resets, delays and pulses all
  appear in executable instruction sets; not every instruction is a unitary.
- **“Every instruction reversible”:** False for full circuits/hardware control. Only ideal coherent gates are unitary;
  measurement/reset/classical control are allowed program instructions.
- **No halt/if:** Dynamic circuits support conditional branches/loops/halt at the classical-control level. Coherent
  conditional logic uses controlled unitaries; quantum Turing machines also formalize halting.
- **In-place update:** Reversible in-place permutations/arithmetic are common; “destructive update” is the prohibited
  operation without preserving information/environment.
- **Branch wording:** Measuring a quantum predicate turns it classical and changes the state; coherent branch selection
  can use quantum control without a classical path.
- **Pure-function analogy:** A unitary is bijective and norm-preserving, not simply a pure function; functional languages
  can express irreversible many-to-one functions, recursion, allocation and effects.
- **Side effects:** Noise/state preparation/reset/discard are additional effects.
- **Wrong forward reference:** It says compiler analog in §34.5, but compilation is in §34.7 (and hardware compilation
  partly here). Correct.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Strong analogy with multiple absolutes needing repair.

#### §34.4 — native gate sets/ISA

- **ISA analogy:** Excellent at compilation-interface level, but vendor “native gates” may be calibrated pulse
  primitives, parameterized operations, echoed sequences or virtual gates rather than fixed hardware instructions.
- **Superconducting set:** \(\{R_Z,\sqrt X,\mathrm{CZ}\}\) is one platform/vendor example; IBM often exposes `rz`, `sx`,
  `x`, and entanglers such as ECR/CZ depending backend. Do not imply a universal typical set.
- **Ion gate:** Mølmer–Sørensen is an XX-type entangler under common phases, not simply “a two-qubit phase gate.”
- **Neutral atoms:** Rydberg blockade gates correct; §20.5 cross-reference needs verification.
- **Fault-tolerant ISA:** Logical machines may expose Clifford+T/lattice surgery rather than physical analog gates; worth
  distinguishing.
- **Escaping:** Replace doubled set escapes.
- **C analogy:** Good, though quantum compilation also depends on calibration snapshot/noise/placement.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Very effective bridge.

#### §34.4 — connectivity/routing

- **Physical connectivity:** Correct for platforms with fixed coupling graphs, but trapped ions/neutral atoms/photonic
  links can offer dynamic/all-to-all/reconfigurable connectivity with different costs.
- **Remote gates:** Compilation may use SWAPs, bridge gates, teleportation, shuttling/movement or native long-range gates;
  SWAP chains are not universal solution.
- **Swap-back:** Often logical-to-physical mapping is allowed to change, so swapping back wastes gates; the text says
  optional, good.
- **Register-allocation analogy:** Qubit placement resembles register allocation, but interference graphs concern
  simultaneous live ranges while coupling graphs constrain two-qubit operations; FPGA placement/routing is closer.
- **“Almost directly”:** Quantum routing includes noncommuting gates, noise/calibration, fidelity, crosstalk and final
  measurement remapping.
- **Chapter 23:** Verify content.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Concrete CNOT example works well.

#### §34.4 — embedded-systems mindset/specs

- **Volatile specs:** Qubit counts, coherence and fidelities require exact 2026 data and platform separation.
- **“Usable qubits”:** Tens to low hundreds is likely stale/ambiguous: devices advertise hundreds/thousands physical
  qubits, while high-quality simultaneously usable application qubits vary. Define.
- **Coherence:** Superconducting hundreds of microseconds and ions seconds are broad ranges; gate times and connectivity
  determine usable depth, not coherence alone.
- **Error-rate range:** \(10^{-3}\)–\(10^{-4}\) cannot describe all one-/two-qubit/readout gates; two-qubit errors often
  differ substantially. Fidelity 0.999–0.9999 arithmetic is correct.
- **Shot counts:** Set by estimation/confidence, queue limits and cost; “measured in thousands” is not a device resource
  limit.
- **Embedded analogy:** Strong attitude analogy, but cloud queues, calibration drift and stochastic outputs differ from
  deterministic microcontrollers.
- **“Every byte”:** Quantum state cannot be managed like addressable bytes.
- **Desktop abstractions luxury:** SDK abstraction is necessary, even on NISQ; compilers may outperform hand tuning.
- **NISQ label:** Time-sensitive and should not define all 2026 engineering.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Highly relatable.

#### §34.5 — shots as Monte Carlo

- **Scope:** Algorithms yielding expectation/probability estimates need repeated shots; deterministic-output algorithms
  can succeed with few repetitions, and mid-circuit protocols differ. “Almost every measurement averaged” is too broad.
- **Variance:** For the sample mean of IID bounded outcomes, variance scales as \(\sigma^2/N\); not simply “variance
  \(1/N\)” without base variance.
- **Digits:** Three additional decimal digits means error reduced \(10^3\), hence \(10^6\) samples under IID Monte Carlo,
  correct assuming statistical error dominates and constants unchanged.
- **Simulated annealing analogy:** It is an optimization Markov chain, not governed universally by standard-error
  \(1/\sqrt N\) in the same sense.
- **Quantum analogs:** Importance sampling/control variates/operator grouping/shadows are distinct techniques; antithetic
  quantum sampling has specialized constructions. Do not claim direct analogs without examples.
- **Cross-references:** Verify §§11.5/11.7.
- **Noise:** Readout/systematic drift creates bias that more shots do not remove.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Digits-to-shots rule is memorable.

#### §34.5 — parameter-shift formula

- **Formula conditions:** For \(e^{-i\theta P/2}\) with \(P^2=I\), the ±\(\pi/2\), factor 1/2 rule is correct for an
  expectation downstream of that gate.
- **Notation:** \(\theta\) is a vector but gate form uses scalar; use \(\boldsymbol\theta\) and shifted unit vector
  consistently. Replace `\\,`.
- **Observable terms/data:** Each \(\langle H\rangle\) may require many Pauli groups, shots and training examples.
- **Repeated parameters:** If the same parameter appears in multiple gates, differentiate each occurrence or use
  generalized rules.
- **Exactness:** Correct analytically; shot estimates remain stochastic.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Strong exact-versus-finite-difference reveal.

#### §34.5 — gradient-cost/backprop comparison

- **\(2p\):** Correct only for one occurrence/two-eigenvalue generator and one aggregate expectation evaluation per
  shift; observable groups/data multiply cost.
- **Backprop false claim:** Reverse-mode AD computes a full scalar-output gradient at a small constant multiple (often
  ~2–5×), not literally one forward pass; it requires a backward pass and cached/recomputed intermediates.
- **“Classical reversibility”:** Backprop exploits chain rule/reverse accumulation, not classical logical reversibility.
- **Quantum caching:** No-cloning prevents saving arbitrary intermediate states; adjoint differentiation can compute
  gradients efficiently on state-vector simulators, and coherent/adjoint quantum gradient methods exist under
  assumptions.
- **Forward-mode analogy wrong:** Parameter shift is coordinate-wise finite-shift evaluation, closer in cost to forward-
  mode/finite differences, but the graph can be rerun from preparation; “cannot re-traverse” is false. It is reexecuted
  for every shift.
- **Worst-case AD:** Loaded phrase; forward mode is efficient for few inputs/many outputs.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Important cost contrast, technical explanation needs rewrite.

#### §34.5 — circuit DAG/depth/width

- **DAG model:** Correct for acyclic static circuits; dynamic loops/classical control and pulse schedules can require
  richer control-flow/event graphs.
- **Edges:** Dependencies include classical outcomes, resource conflicts, crosstalk and calibration constraints, not only
  qubit-time.
- **Depth versus wall-clock:** Gate durations differ, measurements/resets/feed-forward matter, and parallel gates can
  conflict. Weighted scheduled duration, not unweighted depth, governs wall-clock.
- **Width:** Could mean total qubits or maximum live qubits; ancillas/classical bits/resonators matter.
- **EDA analogy:** Strong.
- **CSE:** Arbitrary common subexpression reuse is limited because unknown quantum states cannot be cloned/cached;
  repeated unitary sequences may be synthesized/factored only when dependencies permit.
- **Fidelity model false:** Additional gates do not yield a simple multiplicative fidelity loss under coherent,
  correlated, leakage or mitigated errors; approximate independent stochastic fidelity products are heuristic.
- **Latency:** Extra gates add duration as well as error.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Excellent compiler mental model.

#### §34.6 — ECC RAM analogy

- **Cosmic rays:** DRAM soft errors can come from ionizing radiation and other mechanisms; current scaling/ECC mechanisms
  are more nuanced.
- **SECDED:** A common 72-bit ECC DIMM word uses 64 data +8 parity/check bits for single-error correction/double-error
  detection, but layouts vary and 8-bit count may include overall parity.
- **Quantum error list:** Good; amplitude damping/dephasing/correlated errors/readout errors could be added.
- **Redundancy caveat:** Quantum codes encode into entanglement across physical qubits without copying the unknown state,
  unlike classical repetition/ECC.
- **Structural analogy:** Strong.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Familiar failure-to-redundancy bridge.

#### §34.6 — stabilizer versus Reed–Solomon

- **RS formula wrong/ambiguous:** An \((n,k)\) Reed–Solomon code has distance \(n-k+1\) and corrects
  \(\lfloor(n-k)/2\rfloor\) symbol errors; correct.
- **Quantum formula:** A distance-\(d\) quantum code corrects up to \(\lfloor(d-1)/2\rfloor\) arbitrary errors, correct.
- **“Both linear”:** Stabilizer codes are additive over finite fields/symplectic vector spaces; not simply linear over
  complex amplitudes in the same sense as RS.
- **Decoder claim:** Many decoders are not maximum-likelihood or close approximations in a quantifiable sense; union-
  find, MWPM, BP/OSD, neural decoders trade optimality/scaling.
- **Noisy syndrome:** Classical storage/communication ECC also handles noisy parity checks/decoders, so “no exact
  counterpart” later is overstated; repeated syndrome creates a 3D space-time inference problem.
- **Surface-code cycles:** “Space-time rather than per-cycle” is good.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Effective comparison.

#### §34.6 — threshold theorem

- **Classical attribution:** Von Neumann studied reliable computation from unreliable components; cite exact theorem/model/
  year.
- **Quantum threshold:** Requires local stochastic/Markovian or otherwise bounded noise, fresh ancillas, parallelism,
  fault-tolerant gadgets, locality and sufficiently accurate preparation/measurement; not simply per-gate error.
- **\(10^{-2}\):** Surface-code circuit-level depolarizing thresholds around ~1% are common, but phenomenological/
  biased/leakage/correlated noise and decoder alter it. Do not call one standard value.
- **Overhead statement:** Fault-tolerance threshold theorems often give polylog overhead under ideal architectures/code
  concatenation; 2D locality and practical surface-code space-time overhead require more precise scaling.
- **“Exponential by polynomial”:** Logical error often decreases exponentially in code distance below threshold while
  physical qubits/time grow polynomial/logarithmic in target failure; clarify.
- **Planning logic:** Excellent actionable takeaway.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Strong bridge from theorem to engineering.

#### §34.6 — syndrome/measurement break

- **Classical reading:** Reading a classical bit can be noisy/destructive in some memories and a single observed value
  does not reveal whether it flipped without redundancy; analogy should not idealize.
- **Quantum error detection:** Stabilizers reveal error syndromes without revealing encoded logical amplitudes, but
  measurement projects onto a syndrome subspace and can propagate faults through ancillas.
- **“Bit flip cannot be detected”:** An X error can be detected indirectly; reading the data qubit in Z would indeed
  destroy superposition, which motivates parity checks.
- **No exact counterpart:** Classical parity checks precisely are a counterpart, though quantum noncommutation/
  backaction/no-cloning add differences.
- **Cross-reference:** Verify §34.9.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Good break condition.

#### §34.7 — compiler pipeline

- **Section-title mismatch:** “Physics-Based Modeling Intuition” actually covers software/cloud/probabilistic-programming
  analogies. Rename to “Software Stack and Execution Models” or add actual physics-based modeling.
- **Front end:** Qiskit/Cirq/PennyLane objects are SDK IR/program representations, not uniformly high-level source front
  ends. OpenQASM version matters.
- **Generic IR:** Modern stacks can preserve gates, control flow, timing, classical operations and pulse/calibration
  metadata—not merely generic unitaries/measurements.
- **Middle end:** Good operation list.
- **Back end:** Not every cloud/compiler emits user-visible pulse programs; vendors may lower to proprietary control
  instructions, and fault-tolerant targets may emit logical operations.
- **AWG:** Correct expansion; verify Chapter 21.
- **LLVM analogy:** Strong but “identical” is too absolute; calibration/noise-dependent mapping and probabilistic
  execution make quantum compilation dynamic.
- **Experienced engineer:** Needs quantum semantics/cost/error model and tool architecture; “not a new architecture”
  understates learning.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** High practical value.

#### §34.7 — cloud/GPU analogy

- **CUDA/ROCm category:** CUDA/ROCm are programming/runtime ecosystems, not themselves managed cloud APIs.
- **Job shape:** Circuit/backend/shots/queue/histogram is common, but sessions, samplers/estimators, hybrid jobs,

- **Current product audit:** Qiskit Runtime, Google Quantum AI access/API, Braket and Azure Quantum names/interfaces are
  volatile; verify official 2026 docs. Cirq’s engine may have changed package/API.
- **Launch configuration:** Shot count is repetition count, not strongly analogous to GPU grid/block launch geometry.
- **Transpilation/PTX:** Spelling should be PTX; quantum primitives are estimator/sampler service APIs, not merely renamed
  kernels.
- **Scaling false analogy:** Distributing independent parameter/shot circuits is embarrassingly parallel, but QPU queues,
  drift, access limits, calibration and optimizer feedback differ radically from multi-GPU scaling.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Familiar surface, too confident in transfer.

#### §34.7 — probabilistic-programming analogy

- **State misconception repeated:** A pure quantum state is not a classical probability distribution; it contains
  complex amplitudes and contextual/noncommuting measurement statistics.
- **Unitary determinism:** Correct at ideal state evolution level.
- **Stan/Pyro/Gen:** These express classical probabilistic generative models/inference; they do not model coherent phase/
  interference by ordinary distribution transforms.
- **“Much closer”:** Unsupported ranking; linear algebra, reversible programming, signal processing and probabilistic
  estimation each illuminate different aspects.
- **Patterns that transfer:** Sampling/expectation/variance ideas transfer after measurement, not throughout coherent
  circuit design.
- **Better analogy:** Probabilistic programming is close to hybrid experiment/result modeling, while amplitude
  programming needs complex-linear/interference intuition.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Accessible but conceptually misleading.

#### §34.8 — “transfer almost without modification” framing

- **Core problem:** Every listed intuition needs modification for quantum semantics/noise/hardware. The section’s absolute
  framing contradicts the chapter’s opening promise to mark analogy breaks.
- **Recommendation:** Use “transfer productively, with these adjustments” and append one failure mode to each.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Encouraging, but confidence is too broad.

#### §34.8 — DAG-based reasoning

- **Static circuits:** Dependency graphs/critical paths/parallel independent gates transfer well.
- **Depth:** Unweighted depth is not latency when gate durations differ and measurement/feed-forward/reset/pulses have
  different costs.
- **Width/register pressure:** Qubits are scarce live resources, but quantum width includes ancillas, routing, QEC and
  connectivity; spilling a qubit to memory is not analogous to a register spill.
- **Commutation:** Commuting gates can be reordered mathematically, but calibration, noise, crosstalk, pulse overlap and
  classical dependencies can change physical results.
- **Disjoint gates:** May still conflict through shared controls/readout resonators/crosstalk and hardware concurrency
  limits.
- **“Cleanly”:** Remove.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Highly useful compiler intuition.

#### §34.8 — resource-cost accounting

- **Volatile ratio:** Two-qubit error being 10–100× single-qubit error is not “most platforms” without data; ion/neutral/
  superconducting/photonic operations and virtual Z gates vary radically.
- **Expense dimensions:** Gate infidelity, duration, calibration, connectivity and crosstalk differ; no single cost.
- **T gates:** Often dominate surface-code fault-tolerant cost because magic-state factories are expensive, but alternative
  codes/gate sets/transversal gates/catalysis can shift bottlenecks.
- **Logical qubits:** Physical footprint depends on code, distance, connectivity, target error and architecture.
- **Optimization warning:** “Drive expensive resource down before anything else” can worsen depth, width or logical
  failure. Multiobjective cost functions are required.
- **Embedded discipline:** Strong transfer.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Practical.

#### §34.8 — randomized-algorithm thinking

- **Quantum randomness:** BQP algorithms use coherent amplitudes/interference before measurement, not randomized
  subroutines in the classical sense.
- **Majority vote:** Bounded-error decision algorithms can be amplified by independent repetitions/majority, but many
  algorithms output samples/estimates/factors and use verification/median/maximum-likelihood instead.
- **Class analogy:** BQP and BPP both use bounded error, but BQP is not merely a “quantum analog” operationally.
- **Single-shot “noise”:** Intrinsic outcome randomness is not hardware noise; a single ideal shot may sample the target
  distribution exactly.
- **Tail bounds:** Hoeffding/Chernoff apply to independent bounded classical measurement outcomes. Drift, correlated shots,
  adaptive circuits and quantum-observable estimation require conditions.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Good statistical mindset once randomness/noise are separated.

#### §34.8 — numerical-stability thinking

- **Bad analogy:** Floating-point roundoff is a deterministic/stochastic numerical representation error; quantum gate
  error is a physical channel/coherent control error acting on a state. They do not both simply “compound
  multiplicatively.”
- **Coherent accumulation:** Systematic rotation errors can add in amplitude; stochastic errors may compose roughly in
  probability; leakage/correlation/non-Markovian effects differ.
- **Condition number:** Crucial for HHL/QSVT/linear systems, but not a universal gate-error diagnostic.
- **Mitigation:** Calibration, composite pulses, randomized compiling, error mitigation/correction, robust control and
  algorithm design differ from numerical conditioning.
- **Transfer:** Sensitivity analysis/error budgets/worst-case thinking do transfer strongly.
- **“Almost without modification”:** False.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Useful engineering reflex obscured by overly literal equivalence.

#### §34.8 — layered abstractions

- **Layer stack:** Good, though algorithm may sit between application/circuit, logical/QEC layer is missing, and cloud/
  runtime/control layers matter.
- **Classical mapping:** IR/assembly/microcode/silicon analogy is strong.
- **Layer hiding:** Quantum calibration/noise/connectivity leaks more aggressively; fault-tolerant architectures may
  restore abstraction.
- **Transpiler assumptions:** Placement, optimization level, approximation, calibration snapshot, scheduling, error
  mitigation and target backend should be inspectable/reproducible.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** One of the cleanest transfers.

#### §34.9 — qubit “both values” misconception

- **Correct rejection:** Continuity and relative phase are essential; global phase is redundant.
- **State specification:** A pure qubit is a ray/equivalence class of unit vectors in \(\mathbb C^2\), represented by the
  Bloch sphere; calling it a unit vector is accessible but omits global phase.
- **Proposed replacement still wrong:** “A probability distribution … that can also carry relative phase” is only
  partially adequate. One fixed-basis probability distribution plus relative phase can parameterize a pure qubit, but
  it encourages the classical-mixture model and omits measurement-basis dependence.
- **Better wording:** A coherent complex superposition whose measurement statistics depend on basis and phase.
- **Escaping:** Replace `\\{0,1\\}`.
- **Chapter 35 promise:** Verify.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Essential correction.

#### §34.9 — “parallel brute force” misconception

- **Major false statement:** An arbitrary operation on a length-\(2^n\) amplitude vector does not occur in
  \(O(\mathrm{poly}(n))\). Only circuits composed of polynomially many efficiently implementable local/oracle gates do.
- **Oracle query:** Coherent evaluation over all inputs can be one oracle call, but implementing the oracle and extracting
  a global property determine advantage.
- **Measurement equation:** Correct probability form; formatting around \(\langle x|\psi\rangle\) should be consistent.
- **Interference:** Strong core explanation, though some algorithms exploit entanglement/spectral structure not easily
  summarized as “answers wanted/unwanted.”
- **Deutsch–Jozsa:** It demonstrates query separation for a promise problem, not the best evidence that BQP likely excludes
  NP; verify Chapter 17 reference.
- **Complexity belief:** BQP not known to contain NP-complete problems; “most experts” needs a survey or say “widely
  believed.”
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Vital myth correction.

#### §34.9 — copying/rollback misconception

- **No-cloning:** Correct for arbitrary unknown states; classical basis information and orthogonal sets can be copied.
- **Rollback:** Keeping an entangled checkpoint would not be an independent restorable snapshot and can disrupt
  interference; useful distinction.
- **Uncomputation not rollback:** Uncomputation reverses a known reversible computation, often after extracting output via
  allowed coherent operation. It is not RAII-style recovery from arbitrary destructive execution or measurement.
- **Fault tolerance:** QEC/recovery can correct errors without snapshot copying, providing a different recovery notion.
- **“Never need”:** Too absolute; adaptive algorithms deliberately measure and branch, while fault-tolerant systems
  restore encoded state after detected errors.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Strong software analogy.

#### §34.9 — error/assert misconception

- **Errors not all coherent:** Quantum noise includes coherent, stochastic Pauli, amplitude damping, dephasing, leakage,
  measurement, correlated and non-Markovian components. The opening replaces one false universal with another.
- **Infidelity arithmetic wrong:** A small overrotation angle \(\epsilon\) typically produces infidelity \(O(\epsilon^2)\).
  Two identical coherent overrotations add angles to \(2\epsilon\), giving roughly \(4\) times, not “\(2\epsilon\)
  infidelity.” Opposite/correlated signs can cancel; stochastic errors add approximately.
- **Measurement diagnosis:** Characterization experiments can estimate coherent error across repeated preparations;
  one cannot inspect an in-flight unknown data state freely.
- **Stabilizers:** Measure commuting parity checks using ancillas; checks may not commute with errors but stabilize code
  space. Repeated syndrome plus decoder infers faults.
- **Classical invariant analogy:** Runtime asserts are destructive/control-changing too, while ECC parity checking is the
  closer analog.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Important warning containing a serious quantitative error.

#### §34.9 — branch-on-measurement misconception

- **Dynamic circuits:** Correct that mid-circuit measurement/feed-forward is real and useful.
- **Projection:** Conditional measurement updates entangled subsystems; if measurement outcome is ignored, reduced state
  follows the corresponding channel.
- **“Lose advantage”:** Measurement can create advantage/resource in MBQC, reduce QEC overhead, enable repeat-until-
  success circuits and reset/reuse. It is not inherently harmful.
- **Deferred measurement:** Applies when coherent controls/ancillas can replace measurements and no inaccessible
  classical side effects intervene; it may increase qubits/depth.
- **Hardware advice reversed:** Measurement/feed-forward may be faster/better than coherent long-depth controls on some
  architectures. “Often should” defer requires a cost comparison.
- **Cross-references:** Verify §§9.7/9.9.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Practical, needs balanced hardware guidance.

#### §34.9 — physical versus logical qubits

- **False threshold inference:** A 1% physical error does not mean 1000 qubits yield zero logical qubits. If below the
  relevant threshold, some logical qubits can be encoded, albeit with high logical error/low distance; if at/above
  threshold, scaling distance fails. “Worst case” makes the numeric example meaningless.
- **Second example implausible:** 100 physical qubits at \(10^{-4}\) may encode several tiny logical qubits under some
  codes, but fault-tolerant logical gates/ancillas/factories and target failure determine usefulness. No universal count.
- **Threshold depends:** Gate/readout/leakage/connectivity/noise bias/decoder/cycle schedule matter, not one error rate.
- **Resource metric wrong:** The product “logical-qubit count × logical-gate count × logical fidelity” is not a standard
  monotonic capacity metric; multiplying by more required gates increases the number, falsely suggesting more compute.
  Use logical qubits, achievable logical depth/operations before failure, logical cycle time and total failure budget.
- **Volume metrics:** Quantum volume, algorithmic qubits, CLOPS and logical operations have limitations; Chapter 36 should
  compare them.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Vendor-literacy lesson is crucial, numeric example must be replaced.

#### Chapter 34-to-35 bridge

- **Directness:** Natural transition.
- **Duplication risk:** Chapter 35 gives each misconception fuller treatment; this section should be concise or explicitly
  act as a checklist to avoid repeating entire arguments.
- **Promise audit:** Ensure all six appear in Chapter 35 and corrections agree.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Strong setup.

#### Chapter 34 sanity check 1 — no-cloning/move semantics

- **Good conceptual check:** Expected answer should state no universal operation maps
  \(|\psi\rangle|0\rangle\to|\psi\rangle|\psi\rangle\) for arbitrary unknown \(\psi\).
- **Value/reference wording:** A reference can alias mutable state, whereas move-only ownership better captures transfer
  without duplication; entanglement/nonlocal encoding remains beyond the analogy.
- **“Captures better”:** Loaded but defensible after discussing limits.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Useful.

#### Chapter 34 sanity check 2 — shot count

- **Arithmetic:** Standard error \(\sqrt{\sigma^2/N}=1/\sqrt N=10^{-3}\) gives \(N=10^6\) IID shots.
- **Confidence:** Standard error alone is not a high-confidence absolute-error guarantee; add confidence/observable
  bounds for a tail bound.
- **Classical comparison:** “One floating-point evaluation” is mismatched. A quantum shot includes state preparation/
  circuit/measurement and estimates an expectation; a classical evaluation might compute one deterministic function
  value or one Monte Carlo sample. Compare equivalent estimator tasks.
- **Noise:** Hardware bias means one million shots may not achieve \(10^{-3}\) accuracy.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Memorable scale.

#### Chapter 34 sanity check 3 — parameter shift versus backprop

- **Premise issue:** Backprop has direct quantum analogues in simulators (adjoint differentiation) and coherent quantum
  gradient algorithms under assumptions. Hardware cannot freely cache/copy arbitrary intermediate states, but “no
  direct analog” is too absolute.
- **Expected contrast:** Reverse-mode caches/recomputes classical intermediates and runs a backward pass; parameter shift
  reruns shifted circuits and estimates stochastic expectations.
- **Formula conditions:** Ask readers to state generator condition and cost per observable/data item.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Strong systems question after premise repair.

#### Chapter 34 sanity check 4 — vendor qubit headline

- **Factor wording:** 1000 is 100× 10, not “1000× more than 10 qubits.” The quoted misconception contains an elementary
  arithmetic error unless it means “1000 qubits rather than 10.”
- **Threshold answer:** Physical error below a code/noise-specific threshold permits logical suppression with increased
  distance; above it, adding code size does not drive logical error down.
- **Other factors:** Connectivity, gate/readout fidelity, logical operations, code overhead, yield, calibration, runtime
  and workload mapping.
- **Avoid repeating false examples:** Do not ask readers to infer logical qubits from headline count/error alone.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Excellent vendor-literacy goal.

- **Open-ended/current:** “Recent paper of your choice” requires external research and makes the answer non-reproducible;

- **Layer ambiguity:** Algorithms can span mathematical description, circuit IR and hardware experiments; define layer

- **One layer down:** Changes may include gate decomposition, qubit layout, routing, scheduling, pulses, noise/calibration
  constraints and resource counts.
- **Assessment:** Supply a rubric rather than one answer.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Good applied research task.

#### Chapter 35 title/status/navigation

- **Title:** Accurate and appropriately broad.
- **Status/count:** Fourteen visible numbered sections match `14 / 14`; the file is much longer than neighboring

#### Chapter 35 opening — formalism recap

- **State scope:** Pure states are rays/unit vectors up to global phase; general states are density operators. The recap
  should not erase mixed states after a full book.
- **Gate scope:** Ideal coherent gates are unitaries; general dynamics/noise are quantum channels.
- **Measurement wording:** POVM elements are positive semidefinite operators summing to identity; measurements also need
  an instrument/Kraus operators to specify post-measurement state, not merely “positive operators.”
- **Born rule:** Gives outcome probabilities via \(\operatorname{Tr}(\rho E_i)\); “turns inner products into
  probabilities” covers pure projective cases only.
- **Universal empirical claim:** “Predicts every laboratory outcome the field has ever measured” is indefensible.
  Quantum theory predicts probability distributions under a model; experiments have systematic discrepancies/noise,
  approximations and domains involving QFT/GR/open systems. Say it is extraordinarily well confirmed in tested regimes.
- **Interpretive prediction:** Some objective-collapse/hidden-variable modifications can make different empirical
  predictions, so “nothing in this chapter changes predictions” only applies to interpretations empirically equivalent
  to standard QM.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Strong formalism-first opening.

#### Chapter 35 opening — slogan catalog/thesis

- **Quotes:** Excellent selection of prevalent slogans.
- **“Every one precise”:** Some slogans admit multiple charitable translations rather than one precise translation.
- **Less dramatic:** Operational descriptions may be less sensational, but Bell nonlocality/contextuality remain
  genuinely surprising. Avoid implying all conceptual drama is mere language.
- **Practitioner focus:** Strong and well aligned with book.
- **Line wrapping:** Prose is hard-wrapped unlike some previous chapters; project style consistency should be checked.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Immediately relevant and voiceful.

#### Chapter 35 opening — operational-hygiene goal

- **Interpretation neutrality:** Practitioners can calculate without choosing an ontology; correct.
- **Measurement problem:** Error correction, measurement modeling, quantum control and foundational protocols can require
  operational choices without settling ontology.
- **\(\psi\)-ontic/epistemic gloss:** “Real thing versus someone’s knowledge” is accessible but oversimplifies ontological
  models: \(\psi\)-epistemic means overlapping ontic-state distributions for distinct quantum states, not necessarily
  subjective belief.
- **Pronoun consistency:** “A working practitioner … What they need” is grammatically acceptable singular they.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Clear purpose.

#### Chapter 35 opening — interpretation-zoo claim

- **False universal:** Not all entities commonly grouped into the “interpretations zoo” reproduce exactly the same
  predictions. Bohm, Everett and textbook Copenhagen can be empirically equivalent in ordinary regimes; GRW/CSL are
  modified dynamics with testable deviations; superdeterministic/retrocausal models may have differing auxiliary
  structure.
- **Experiment statement:** Empirically equivalent interpretations cannot be distinguished by existing standard-QM
  predictions, but future theories/extensions or precise collapse tests can discriminate models. “Cannot be settled by
  experiment alone” is too categorical.
- **Recommendation:** Separate interpretations of fixed formalism from alternative physical theories.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Sets up an important distinction the chapter must honor.

#### §35.1 — popular “parallel evaluation” claim

- **Target misconception:** Correct and important.
- **State preparation:** The displayed state arises by preparing a uniform input register and coherently querying a
  reversible oracle \(U_f\); constructing that oracle may dominate cost.
- **Normalization/output width:** If \(f(x)\) is multi-bit, define the output register; normalization is correct over
  \(2^n\) inputs.
- **Measurement:** Measuring both registers yields uniformly random \(x\) and its \(f(x)\) for the ideal displayed state,
  correct, even when multiple \(x\) share outputs.
- **“Holds values”:** The state encodes correlations in amplitudes/basis labels but not \(2^n\) independently addressable
  classical records.
- **“Access not real”:** Access is restricted, not nonexistent; global observables/interference can reveal properties.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Crisp demolition with one equation.

#### §35.1 — interference as engine

- **Core insight:** Structured interference is a much better default account than parallel worlds/evaluations.
- **Over-universalization:** Quantum speedups can also be framed through spectral estimation, entanglement, query
  complexity, quantum walks, tunneling or sampling hardness; all rely on amplitude dynamics but not always a clean
  wrong-cancels/right-reinforces story.
- **Wrong/right answers:** Algorithms estimating phases/distributions need not have discrete “wrong answers.”
- **Classical analogy:** Signed/complex Monte Carlo or wave interference is closer than “negative probabilities.”
  Classical waves also have complex amplitudes and cancellation, while quantum measurement/resource scaling differs.
- **“Cancellations are real”:** Ambiguous—amplitudes can be complex; cancellation affects observable probabilities.
- **Cross-reference:** Verify Chapter 10 §10.2.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Strong replacement metaphor.

#### §35.1 — diagnostic question/examples

- **Excellent question:** It forces authors to identify the extraction mechanism and is highly reusable.
- **Measurement exception:** Sampling tasks can have quantum value precisely by measuring a prepared distribution that
  is hard to sample classically; “we just measure” can be a valid algorithm if state preparation itself creates a
  classically hard distribution. Boson/random-circuit sampling are direct counterexamples.
- **Encoded distribution:** Even without later amplification, efficiently preparing a distribution unavailable
  classically may be the benefit.
- **Deutsch–Jozsa:** Final Hadamards reveal a global parity/orthogonality promise, but “amplifies” is loose.
- **Grover terminology:** Uses phase oracle plus diffusion/inversion about the mean; “reflection-and-inversion” is
  redundant/vague.
- **Phase estimation:** Inverse QFT converts phase to a bitstring distribution; correct.
- **Shor:** Period finding applies QFT/inverse-QFT depending convention to a periodic superposition after modular
  exponentiation/measurement; verify wording.
- **Readability:** Avoid line break splitting quoted \(2^n\)-fold phrase.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Named algorithms sustain momentum.

#### §35.1 — replacement slogan

- **Merit:** “Structured interference” is concise, memorable and accurate for many algorithms.
- **Scope:** Add “or deliberately engineered quantum sampling statistics” so the slogan does not exclude sampling
  advantage.
- **Marketing aside:** Light humor works.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Strong ending.

#### Chapter 35 checkpoint after §35.1

- **Coverage added:** Every paragraph/equation/example in §35.1 is reviewed.
- **Strongest issue:** The diagnostic rule incorrectly says mere measurement cannot be an algorithm, overlooking quantum-
  sampling tasks whose prepared output distribution itself is classically hard.
- **Status:** Second pass remains in progress for this manuscript file; resume at §35.2.

#### §35.2 — “spooky action” framing

- **Historical attribution:** Einstein’s “spooky action at a distance” wording is commonly attributed through a 1947
  letter to Born; verify exact source/translation and avoid calling it simply a complaint without context.
- **Mechanism versus update:** In collapse-language accounts, measuring A changes the conditional state assigned to B;
  operationally no controllable local statistic changes at B. The paragraph should distinguish ontology from signaling,
  not declare that nothing “does something.”
- **Distance:** No-signaling applies to spacelike-separated choices/outcomes; causal influences can propagate within
  light cones.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Familiar puzzle immediately engages.

#### §35.2 — reduced-state assertion

- **Contradictory outcome wording:** Bob’s *unconditional accessible* reduced state is independent of Alice’s choice of
  trace-preserving local operation. Bob’s state conditioned on a particular Alice outcome generally does depend on that
  outcome, as the final paragraph admits. Do not say \(\rho_B\) is “independent … of what outcome she got” without
  explicitly averaging/denying outcome access.
- **Measurement choice:** No-signaling holds for any local quantum instrument when the outcomes are ignored, not because
  all conditional states are equal.
- **Initial correlations:** Bob’s original marginal can of course depend on how the joint state was prepared; the claim
  concerns Alice’s later local choice.
- **Cross-reference:** Verify §10.6 uses correct instrument formalism.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Clean concept, internally inconsistent.

#### §35.2 — POVM equation

- **Equation is wrong/ambiguous:** POVM effects \(M_a\) are positive operators summing to \(I\), but post-measurement
  unnormalized states are not generally
  \(\operatorname{Tr}_A[(M_a\otimes I)\rho]\) as a state-update rule unless exploiting a partial-trace identity solely for
  outcome probabilities/marginal. A general instrument uses Kraus operators
  \(K_{a\mu}\rho K_{a\mu}^\dagger\).
- **Missing dagger:** If \(M_a\) denotes a measurement Kraus operator, the expression must contain
  \((M_a\otimes I)\rho(M_a^\dagger\otimes I)\) and completeness
  \(\sum_a M_a^\dagger M_a=I\).
- **Correct proof:** Summing the unnormalized Bob states over all outcomes of a trace-preserving local instrument yields
  \(\rho_B\); show that explicitly.
- **General local operation:** Alice can include ancillas/unitaries/noise/measurement; any CPTP map on A leaves B’s
  marginal invariant.
- **Escaping:** Replace doubled braces/spacing.
- **Severity:** This is a strong correctness defect in the central formal proof.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The equation should be the section’s trust anchor.

#### §35.2 — Bell records/information flow

- **Bell correlations:** Joint correlations require comparing records, correct.
- **Local statistics:** Each party can observe local randomness immediately, but cannot infer the other’s setting/outcome
  from it.
- **Loopholes:** Bell-test inference depends on spacelike setting choices, detection/event-ready sampling and statistical
  assumptions; “Bell-tested” is fine at overview level.
- **“Entire information flow”:** Quantum systems/photons used to distribute entanglement travel subluminally too; classical
  record comparison is not the only physical flow in experiment preparation.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Strong operational statement.

#### §35.2 — replacement slogan

- **Terminology:** “Nonlocal correlation” means violation of Bell-local hidden-variable models, not a directly measurable
  faster-than-light influence. Define to avoid recreating the misconception.
- **Relativity:** Standard quantum theory respects operational no-signaling, but reconciling nonlocal correlations with
  relativistic causal explanation is conceptually subtler than “relativity demands.”
- **Theorem:** No-signaling follows from local CPTP operations/tensor-product structure plus Born rule.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Memorable and standard.

#### §35.2 — conditional-state clarification

- **Best paragraph:** This correctly distinguishes conditional and unconditional states and should precede/fix the
  earlier reduced-state assertion.
- **Conditioning:** Alice need not always send the literal outcome immediately; Bob can sort already-recorded data after
  receiving setting/outcome metadata. No local real-time signal appears.
- **Steering:** Different Alice measurements can remotely prepare different ensembles with the same Bob marginal
  (quantum steering); naming this would deepen the point.
- **Envelope analogy limitation:** Correlated cards model classical common-cause correlations and cannot reproduce Bell-
  inequality violations across freely chosen measurement settings. It illustrates conditioning versus signaling only,
  not quantum nonlocality.
- **“Nothing traveled”:** The correlated cards were physically distributed earlier, analogous to entanglement
  distribution; good.
- **Choice of when:** Also cannot signal by choosing measurement basis/outcome; timing alone example is narrower.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Excellent intuition if its Bell limitation is explicit.

#### §35.3 — projective-collapse postulate

- **Scope:** \(P_m|\psi\rangle/\sqrt{p(m)}\) is the ideal projective pure-state Lüders update, with
  \(p(m)=\langle\psi|P_m|\psi\rangle\). General POVMs require an instrument/Kraus operators and can yield mixed states.
- **Degeneracy:** Lüders versus von Neumann refinements can differ for degenerate projectors; optional advanced caveat.
- **“After observing”:** Operationally condition on a registered outcome; observer consciousness is not part of the
  formal rule.
- **Popular reading:** Textbook collapse formulations do posit nonunitary state update, while objective-collapse theories
  explicitly modify dynamics. Calling this merely “popular” understates legitimate formal positions.
- **Switch condition:** The measurement problem indeed concerns the cut/conditions in textbook dual dynamics.
- **Cross-references:** Verify Postulate 3 and Schrödinger section.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Directly engages a central conceptual fault line.

#### §35.3 — Bayesian/conditional-update proposal

- **Interpretive bias:** Calling observer-description conditionalization “narrower and more defensible” advocates an
  epistemic/operational reading despite the chapter’s claimed neutrality. It is a useful calculational stance, not a
  settled theorem.
- **Quantum versus classical Bayes:** Quantum instruments physically disturb systems and update both probabilities and
  states; the analogy to Bayesian conditioning is incomplete.
- **State role:** A quantum state predicts intervention-dependent measurement statistics and transformations, not merely
  a passive generator.
- **Relative-state nuance:** Different interpretations explain the conditional state differently; Everett uses relative
  branches, Bohm conditional/effective wavefunctions, objective collapse physical dynamics.
- **Good sentence:** The final sentence correctly locates physical-versus-informational status inside the measurement
  problem and partly repairs the opening bias.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Clear and philosophically charged.

#### §35.3 — unread measurement/mixed state

- **“Always relative”:** This is interpretation-dependent. Operational state assignments are information-relative, but
  ontic theories may assign observer-independent states/variables.
- **Unlearned outcome:** If outcome is ignored/unavailable, the observer predicts with the nonselective post-measurement
  channel \(\rho'=\sum_m P_m\rho P_m\), generally a mixed/dephased state—not necessarily the same as the premeasurement
  state.
- **“Not a collapsed one”:** Misleading: it is an ensemble/nonselective mixture of conditional collapsed states under
  collapse language. “Not conditioned on one outcome” is precise.
- **Physical record:** A measurement apparatus/environment becomes correlated and decoherence occurs whether a human
  learns the record.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Important observer-information distinction.

#### §35.3 — QEC application

- **Reason is misstated:** Syndrome measurements are designed to reveal error-subspace information while revealing no
  logical-state information. Encoded data is not “unaffected”: the state is projected into a syndrome sector, errors
  remain until corrected/tracked, and faulty checks can damage data.
- **Outcome knowledge:** QEC requires syndrome outcomes to choose/update correction/Pauli frame; unread outcomes would
  leave a mixture of error sectors and generally cannot protect computation.
- **Information leakage:** No *logical* information should leak; syndrome/error information deliberately enters the
  classical record.
- **Backaction:** Stabilizer measurements commute with logical operators/code subspace ideally, explaining preservation
  better than observer relativity.
- **Severity:** Strong conceptual defect because it uses QEC as proof of an incorrect “outcome not learned” claim.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Practical connection is excellent after correction.

#### §35.3 — unanswered mechanism questions

- **Standard QM:** Textbook formalism does not specify physical collapse speed/trigger beyond measurement postulate/cut;
  correct.
- **Testable alternatives:** GRW/CSL and related objective-collapse models *do* specify rates/triggers and are
  experimentally constrained. These questions are scientific under modified theories, not inherently confused.
- **Decoherence:** Explains effective suppression of interference/records but not unique outcome; later section should
  connect.
- **“Wrong direction”:** Unjustified and polemical. Physical collapse is one possible modified-theory direction,
  empirically constrained but not logically declared wrong by standard operational formalism.
- **Unresolved:** Correct and important.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** The unanswered-question list is compelling.

#### §35.3 — replacement slogan

- **Operational value:** “Conditional update” is excellent for calculations.
- **Scope label:** Say it is the operational rule regardless of interpretation, not a metaphysical correction proving no
  physical collapse.
- **Math unchanged:** For interpretations of standard QM, yes; objective-collapse models change mathematics/predictions.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Concise.

#### §35.4 — measurement-disturbance misconception

- **Core distinction:** Preparation uncertainty and measurement error/disturbance are distinct; excellent.
- **“Simultaneously measure”:** Joint measurability, sequential measurements and preparation uncertainty are separate
  questions. The popular sentence conflates all three.
- **Historical nuance:** Heisenberg’s original microscope discussion involved disturbance, while Kennard/Robertson
  formalized preparation uncertainty. Title should avoid implying Heisenberg never discussed disturbance.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Clear misconception target.

#### §35.4 — Robertson relation/equation

- **State scope:** The displayed pure-state Robertson relation is correct for self-adjoint observables/domains where
  moments and commutator are defined. Generalize to density operators if chapter claims “any state.”
- **Escaping:** Replace `\\,`.
- **Definition:** \(\Delta A\) should explicitly be standard deviation
  \(\sqrt{\langle(A-\langle A\rangle)^2\rangle}\); formula is equivalent.
- **Fresh copies:** Operational estimation typically uses ensembles of identically prepared copies, but the mathematical
  variances are properties of one state/distribution and need not be framed as two literal different copies.
- **Continuous observables:** Position/momentum require domain care; for them Kennard gives \(\Delta x\Delta p\ge\hbar/2\).
- **Stronger relation:** Schrödinger–Robertson includes covariance/anticommutator and avoids some zero-RHS weakness.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Good formal anchor.

#### §35.4 — “noncommuting means no simultaneous sharp state”

- **Overstatement:** Two operators that do not commute globally can still share some eigenvectors in dimensions greater
  than two, so a particular state can have \(\Delta A=\Delta B=0\) even when \([A,B]\ne0\) as an operator. No common
  eigenbasis/joint sharpness for all states is the safer statement.
- **Robertson RHS:** The expectation \(\langle[A,B]\rangle\) can vanish in a state even for noncommuting operators,
  yielding a trivial bound.
- **Canonical pair:** Position/momentum have no normalizable simultaneous eigenstate, a stronger specific result.
- **State/algebra thesis:** Correct after quantifier repair.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Important conceptual point presently too absolute.

#### §35.4 — error–disturbance literature

- **Distinction:** Excellent to name Ozawa/Branciard rather than deny disturbance theory.
- **Citations:** Verify years, exact inequalities and experimental status from primary/review sources.
- **Terminology:** Define measurement error and disturbance operationally; several inequivalent definitions exist.
- **“Active”:** Current-status claim needs cutoff but is plausible.
- **History:** Avoid implying the textbook product \(\epsilon(A)\eta(B)\ge|\langle[A,B]\rangle|/2\) is universally valid;
  Ozawa famously corrected/extended it.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Adds intellectual depth.

#### §35.4 — Pauli eigenstate example

- **Numerical result:** For \(|0\rangle\), \(\Delta Z=0\), \(\Delta X=\Delta Y=1\); correct.
- **Faulty justification:** The commutators alone do not yield these values through the displayed Robertson bound.
  In \(|0\rangle\), \(\langle Y\rangle=\langle X\rangle=0\), so both RHS commutator expectations cited are zero and the
  inequalities are trivial. Calculate \(X^2=Y^2=I\) and zero means directly.
- **X–Y relation:** \([X,Y]=2iZ\) gives \(\Delta X\Delta Y\ge|\langle Z\rangle|=1\), saturated by \(|0\rangle\), which is
  the useful commutator for this example.
- **“Maximal”:** For Pauli observables with eigenvalues ±1, standard deviation is at most one; state this normalization.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Excellent example with the wrong algebraic explanation.

#### §35.4 — “has sharp value” wording

- **Interpretive caution:** An eigenstate–eigenvalue link is common, but saying an unmeasured qubit “has” a value is
  interpretation-sensitive, especially in a chapter policing ontology.
- **Operational phrasing:** A Z measurement is predictable with probability one; X outcomes are equiprobable.
- **Y omitted:** The preceding sentence mentions Y but final explanation only X; optionally include it.
- **Same-state claim:** No state has zero variance for two distinct Pauli axes; correct for qubits.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Accessible.

  wording are separately reviewed.
- **Strongest issues:** Global noncommutation is incorrectly said to forbid every common sharp state, and the Pauli
  example cites commutators whose expectation values give a zero bound rather than proving \(\Delta X=\Delta Y=1\).

#### §35.5 — thought-experiment framing

- **German plural:** *Gedankenexperimente* is correct German plural but may feel performative; “thought experiments” is
  clearer for the book’s audience.
- **“Technical content worn smooth”:** Excellent motivation.
- **Page-space claim:** Rendering-dependent; say attention/space.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Strong setup.

#### §35.5 — cat apparatus/state

- **Original scenario:** Include Geiger counter/relay/hammer timing if historical fidelity matters; the simplified
  nucleus-vial chain is adequate.
- **Half-life amplitude:** Equal amplitudes follow only in an ideal two-outcome decay/no-decay model after one half-life,
  ignoring emitted particles/environment and phases.
- **State labels:** The displayed state omits apparatus/environment and treats macroscopically broad alive/dead subspaces
  as pure orthogonal kets. Label it schematic.
- **Normalization:** Correct.
- **Entanglement:** It is a coherent entangled superposition, not merely classical correlation; later prose must preserve
  that distinction.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Iconic and concise.

#### §35.5 — cat interpretation

- **Overcorrection:** Saying the state only “assigns probabilities” and does not say the cat occupies both configurations
  risks replacing a pure coherent superposition with an incoherent mixture. Relative phase/interference distinguishes
  them, in principle.
- **Basis dependence:** Correct but not sufficient: alive/dead is selected as a robust pointer basis by system–
  environment interactions, making it physically privileged approximately.
- **Ontology neutrality:** Whether both branches/configurations exist is precisely interpretation-dependent; the
  formalism supplies amplitudes/correlations, not the categorical denial stated.
- **Original purpose:** Schrödinger introduced the cat partly as a reductio/critique of naïvely extending quantum-state
  superpositions to macroscopic reality, not merely a neutral boundary prompt.
- **Macroscopic superpositions:** Standard formalism permits them subject to Hamiltonian/superselection constraints;
  experiments have created mesoscopic/macroscopic superpositions under various measures.
- **Decoherence:** Does more than “suppress it to undetectability”: environmental entanglement suppresses reduced-state
  coherences in a pointer basis but does not select one unique outcome.
- **Measurement problem:** Correct central takeaway.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Strong, philosophically too decisive.

#### §35.5 — EPR history/state

- **Historical precision:** Original EPR used continuous position/momentum correlations; Bohm later recast it with spin.
  The parenthetical acknowledges this, but say EPR’s *argument in Bohm form* rather than “considering the Bell state.”
- **Singlet correlations:** Measurements along the same axis are perfectly anticorrelated; “every shared basis” is
  reasonable for spin directions but basis conjugation conventions for arbitrary qubit bases deserve care.
- **EPR criterion:** Their argument invoked a criterion of reality plus locality/separability to infer elements of
  reality and incompleteness; “must reflect pre-existing values” compresses the logic.
- **Action phrase:** Quote/paraphrase historically carefully.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Excellent bridge from 1935 to Bell.

#### §35.5 — Bell/CHSH conclusion

- **CHSH scope:** Local hidden-variable theories obey \(|S|\le2\); quantum maximum is Tsirelson’s
  \(2\sqrt2\). Experiments approach/violate 2, not generically “give exactly \(2\sqrt2\)” due noise/settings/statistics.
- **Bell theorem logic:** “Locality, realism, or measurement independence” is a popular but disputed trilemma. Bell
  locality/factorizability includes assumptions often decomposed into parameter/outcome independence; “realism” is not
  necessarily an independent premise.
- **Other assumptions:** Freedom/measurement independence, causal arrow, no-conspiracy, detector/event independence and
  applicability of probability theory enter different derivations/loopholes.
- **Textbook realism claim:** Copenhagen-like readings deny pre-existing values for incompatible observables, but many
  accounts instead emphasize Bell local causality; Bohm retains realism with nonlocality. Do not call one “the textbook”
  resolution.
- **§35.13 preview:** It apparently covers measurement independence/free will; ensure it does not imply this is the only
  alternative to anti-realism.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** High-stakes, requires philosophical precision.

#### §35.5 — Wigner’s friend setup

- **Conditional descriptions:** Friend uses a conditional outcome state; Wigner may assign an entangled state if the lab
  is isolated and he treats it unitarily.
- **“Both correct”:** This is a relational/perspectival interpretive stance, not an interpretation-neutral consequence.
  Objective-collapse theories, single-world Copenhagen cuts and Everettian accounts explain the assignments differently.
- **Physical feasibility:** Wigner’s interference measurement on a macroscopic friend/lab is fantastically difficult;
  thought experiment assumes coherence/reversibility.
- **Information versus fact:** Different state assignments from different information can be operationally consistent
  under quantum theory, but whether there is one observer-independent event is the issue, not an “only apparent”
  inconsistency already resolved.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Naturally provocative.

#### §35.5 — Frauchiger–Renner/Bong claim

- **Citation audit:** Verify 2018 publication/version/title and Bong et al. 2020 “local friendliness” theorem. Bong is not
  simply a refinement of FR; it derives experimentally testable inequalities under distinct assumptions.
- **Assumption statement:** FR’s advertised assumptions are often labeled quantum theory (Q), single-world consistency
  (S), and consistency of agents’ reasoning (C), with protocol/inference subtleties. The text’s three paraphrases may not
  match them.
- **Contested theorem:** Extensive literature disputes inference rules, certainty transfer, conditioning and operational
  implementability. Present strongest criticisms rather than one settled takeaway.
- **“Contradiction with standard theory”:** FR shows a set of assumptions cannot all hold in its ideal scenario, not that
  simply combining actual records under ordinary lab practice contradicts QM.
- **Classical reasoning phrase:** “Reason classically about each other” is vague; agents use quantum predictions plus a
  consistency rule.
- **Outcome fact:** Observer-independent facts/local friendliness and single-world outcome are related but not identical.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** Fascinating, very dense.

#### §35.5 — practitioner takeaway

- **Observer in formalism:** Operational quantum theory explicitly includes agents’ interventions, settings, outcomes/
  records, while the microscopic ontology does not define conscious observer as a special dynamical primitive.
- **Measurement instruments:** A practitioner must model where quantum systems couple to classical control/readout; the
  “observer” can be replaced by an instrument/record, but not ignored.
- **Paradox claim:** Treating observer as primitive is not the sole cause of FR/Wigner paradoxes; assumptions about
  universal unitarity, facts, consistency and locality matter.
- **Practical value:** Keep state assignments explicitly conditioned on available records and avoid mixing incompatible
  experimental contexts.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** Useful if made operational.
