  except for oracle labeling; no project generator reference or intrinsic accessible description is present.
- **Accessibility:** No title/description/ARIA semantics states the constant-versus-balanced promise or how measurement
  decides it.
- **Preparation:** H on the three query qubits and X then H on the implicit-zero ancilla correctly prepare the standard
  Deutsch–Jozsa input with the ancilla in \(|-\rangle\).
- **Oracle:** A four-wire \(U_f\) is correct for
  \(|x,y\rangle\mapsto|x,y\oplus f(x)\rangle\), but the promise that \(f\) is either constant or balanced exists nowhere
  in the image. The circuit is uninterpretable without that contract.
- **Decision rule:** H and measurement on the three query qubits are correct: ideal outcome \(000\) means constant;
  any nonzero outcome means balanced. That decisive payoff should appear in the caption or as a compact output brace.
- **One-sided inference:** A particular nonzero string does not identify a generic balanced function; it only certifies
  “not constant” under the promise. Avoid visual proximity to Bernstein–Vazirani that suggests the measured string is a
  hidden answer in both algorithms.
- **Ancilla:** It is correctly left unmeasured because it carries no needed output. Naming it `ancilla` rather than only
  \(q_3\) would explain the asymmetry.
- **Bit order:** The all-zero versus nonzero test is invariant under bit reversal, so endianness is less dangerous here
  than in Bernstein–Vazirani; it still matters for interpreting a displayed nonzero example.
- **Oracle ports/barriers:** White `0–3` labels can be mistaken for data, while two heavy gray barriers encode stage
  grouping without naming the stages. Use “prepare / query / interfere” labels or whitespace.
- **Similarity risk:** Because this figure differs visibly from Bernstein–Vazirani only in \(U_f\) versus \(U_s\), side-
  by-side presentation could either teach a valuable shared template or feel accidentally duplicated. Explicitly
  compare their different promise and readout semantics.
- **Visual clarity:** Render is clean and unclipped, with strong gate/oracle hierarchy; small register indices remain the
  weakest legibility point.
- **Improvement:** Add semantic metadata/provenance, name query and ancilla registers, define the oracle promise, put the
  decision rule at the output, and label conceptual stages.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The single-query classification is compelling, though the image omits the result that creates
  the surprise.
- **Completion:** Entire SVG source and browser rendering inspected.

#### `book/part-06-algorithms/figures/grover-iteration.svg` — source, semantics and rendered appearance

- **Source:** 976-line, very wide Matplotlib 3.10.9/Qiskit-style SVG with three wires and a fully decomposed oracle plus
  diffuser; no intrinsic description or project regeneration pointer exists.
- **Accessibility:** No title/description/ARIA semantics communicates the marked state, phase inversion or amplitude-
  amplification role.
- **Initialization:** H on all three implicit-zero inputs correctly prepares the uniform eight-state superposition.
- **Oracle correctness:** H–CCX–H on \(q_2\) implements CCZ and flips the phase of \(|111\rangle\), so this is not a
  generic “oracle” but a specific marker for the all-ones state. The marked state must be named.
- **Diffuser correctness:** \(H^{\otimes3}X^{\otimes3}\), H–CCX–H on the final qubit, then
  \(X^{\otimes3}H^{\otimes3}\) implements the usual inversion-about-the-mean operator up to an irrelevant global phase.
- **Iteration naming:** The initial uniform-superposition H layer is preparation, not normally part of each repeated
  Grover iterate. Calling the entire asset “Grover iteration” risks suggesting those first H gates repeat.
- **Stage labels:** `oracle` and `diffuser` sit above gray barriers at their left boundaries. The labels visually attach
  to the divider rather than span the operations they name, and the oracle label does not disclose the marked item.
- **No measurement:** Omitting readout is valid for a circuit illustrating one iterate, but surrounding prose must say
  that the oracle–diffuser pair repeats an optimized number of times before measurement.
- **Iteration-count nuance:** With \(N=8,M=1\), one iteration improves success substantially but is not exact certainty;
  two are nearer optimal. Avoid implying the shown single iterate guarantees \(|111\rangle\).
- **Resource hiding:** CCX symbols conceal costly decompositions and connectivity overhead; this is appropriate
  algorithmically but not for hardware-depth claims.
- **Visual width:** The render is clean and logically ordered, yet extreme horizontal aspect ratio will force small
  gates or overflow on narrow pages. Split into labeled preparation/oracle/diffuser panels or use boxed abstractions plus
  a separate decomposition.
- **Color/contrast:** Gate types remain recognizable by labels and shapes, not color alone. Gray barriers are visually
  heavier than their pedagogical value.
- **Improvement:** Add intrinsic semantics/provenance, explicitly label marked \(|111\rangle\), bracket the three stages,
  clarify which portion repeats, and state the success probability or amplitude change after one iterate.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** The concrete transformation has real mechanical drama; a small amplitude-before/after inset
  would make the payoff even more vivid.
- **Completion:** Entire SVG source and browser rendering inspected.

#### `book/part-06-algorithms/figures/qft-3qubit.svg` — source, semantics and rendered appearance

- **Source:** 524-line Matplotlib 3.10.9/Qiskit-style SVG showing three H gates, three controlled phases and a terminal
  SWAP; it has neither project generator provenance nor intrinsic accessibility metadata.
- **Accessibility:** No title/description/ARIA semantics communicates operation order, angles or final bit reversal.
- **Sequence correctness:** Read left to right, the circuit applies H on \(q_0\), controlled phases \(\pi/2\) from the
  \(q_0/q_1\) pair and \(\pi/4\) from \(q_0/q_2\), then H on \(q_1\), controlled phase \(\pi/2\) on \(q_1/q_2\), H on
  \(q_2\), and SWAP \(q_0\leftrightarrow q_2\). This is a standard three-qubit QFT decomposition under the intended
  little-endian/wire convention.
- **Convention sensitivity:** Reversing tensor or wire significance reverses the apparent gate order, control direction
  and need for terminal swaps. The caption must explicitly bind \(q_0\) to least/most significant status and define the
  QFT sign convention.
- **Controlled-phase notation:** Symmetric paired cyan dots correctly reflect the symmetry of a controlled phase, but
  the nearby label `P (π/2)` can look like a one-qubit P gate floating between wires. Use `CP(π/2)` or a legend.
- **Label placement:** The \(\pi/2\) and \(\pi/4\) labels sit beside/below connectors at small type, inconsistently close
  to different wires; they will be difficult to read after reduction.
- **Bit reversal:** The final cross pair clearly shows a SWAP, yet its purpose is unstated. Explain that it restores the
  chosen output order and may be omitted when later classical interpretation reverses bits.
- **Mathematical scope:** The figure shows a unitary decomposition but no formula
  \(|x\rangle\mapsto2^{-3/2}\sum_k e^{2\pi i xk/8}|k\rangle\) or phase-gradient intuition. A caption should connect the
  mechanics to the transform rather than expecting symbol recognition.
- **Approximation opportunity:** On larger QFTs, small-angle rotations may be dropped; noting that \(\pi/4\) is the
  smallest angle here would prepare readers for approximate QFT and noise tradeoffs.
- **Visual width:** Render is unclipped and far less crowded than the Grover asset, though generous horizontal spacing
  and tiny phase labels produce an imbalanced information density.
- **Color/contrast:** H and SWAP remain recognizable without color. The light-cyan controlled-phase connectors have
  weaker contrast than black wires and should be tested for print/grayscale.
- **Improvement:** Add semantic metadata/provenance, explicit QFT/endianness/sign conventions, `CP` labels with larger
  angles, and a note explaining the terminal bit reversal.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The descending phase pattern and final swap are elegant, but a phase-gradient annotation would
  make the underlying structure more delightful.
- **Completion:** Entire SVG source and browser rendering inspected.

#### `book/part-08-noise-and-qec/figures/bit-flip-code.svg` — source, semantics and rendered appearance

- **Source:** 846-line Matplotlib 3.10.9/Qiskit-style SVG with three data wires, two ancillas, two syndrome bits, an
  encoding block and parity measurements; no intrinsic semantics or regeneration pointer is included.
- **Accessibility:** No title/description/ARIA role explains the codewords, stabilizer checks or syndrome meaning.
- **Encoding correctness:** CNOTs \(d_0\to d_1\) and \(d_0\to d_2\), with \(d_1,d_2\) initially zero, map
  \(\alpha|0\rangle+\beta|1\rangle\) to \(\alpha|000\rangle+\beta|111\rangle\), the three-qubit repetition encoding
  against bit flips.
- **Syndrome extraction:** CNOTs from \(d_0,d_1\) into \(a_0\) measure \(Z_0Z_1\) parity, while CNOTs from \(d_1,d_2\)
  into \(a_1\) measure \(Z_1Z_2\) parity, assuming ancillas begin in \(|0\rangle\). This is correct for X-error
  detection.
- **Syndrome table absent:** The image does not map `00, 10, 11, 01` (subject to displayed bit order) to no error and
  flips on \(d_0,d_1,d_2\). Without that table, the measured bits have no operational meaning.
- **Scope/title risk:** The figure shows encoding and syndrome measurement, not correction, decoding or a complete
  fault-tolerant bit-flip-code cycle. A filename/title of “bit-flip code” is broader than the actual circuit.
- **No injected error:** There is no X error or noise interval between encoding and extraction. This keeps the template
  general but makes the syndrome mechanism abstract; a highlighted example error would improve intuition.
- **Ancilla reset/reuse:** One-shot fresh ancillas are implied. Repeated error correction would require reset,
  measurement scheduling and protection against propagation; do not let this diagram imply a full repeated cycle.
- **Quantum limitation:** The repetition code corrects a single X error but not arbitrary phase errors. Pairing this
  figure with the no-cloning-compatible encoding argument and its distance \(d=3\) scope is essential.
- **Stage labeling:** `encode` is placed above the barrier *after* the two encoding CNOTs, which may read as labeling the
  following syndrome block. Put the word over a bracket spanning the actual encoding gates.
- **Visual clarity:** Five wires remain surprisingly readable, control-target relationships are clean, and data/ancilla
  labels help. Long unlabelled regions and the heavy barrier reduce information density.
- **Classical order:** Syndrome destinations `0/1` and width `2` are tiny SDK metadata; any printed syndrome table must
  reconcile register-display order explicitly.
- **Improvement:** Add semantic metadata/provenance, initial states and stage brackets, stabilizer labels \(Z_0Z_1\) and
  \(Z_1Z_2\), an error-to-syndrome table, and a clear statement that recovery is not shown.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The circuit makes redundancy and parity extraction tangible; an animated or highlighted
  single-error path would turn it into a stronger detective story.
- **Completion:** Entire SVG source and browser rendering inspected.

#### `book/part-08-noise-and-qec/figures/filter-functions.svg` — source, semantics and rendered appearance

- **Source:** 2,442-line Matplotlib 3.11.0 SVG containing dense sampled paths for Ramsey, Hahn echo and CPMG-4 on log-log
  axes. It has some live `<text>` annotations but no title/description/ARIA semantics or project generator pointer.
- **Accessibility:** Legend colors are supplemented by distinct solid/dashed/dash-dot styles, good, but no intrinsic
  description conveys the qualitative comparison or equations behind the curves.
- **Axes:** Horizontal \(\omega t/2\pi\) and vertical \(F(\omega,t)/t^2\) are dimensionless under the intended
  normalization. The text/caption should define total sequence duration \(t\) and the exact filter-function convention,
  since factors of \(2\), \(\pi\) and \(\omega^2\) vary across literature.
- **Low-frequency behavior:** Ramsey/free evolution remains high toward DC, whereas Hahn echo and CPMG-4 suppress slow
  components. The annotation “free evolution passes slow noise” correctly captures the dephasing vulnerability.
- **Pulse-count behavior:** The principal passband shifts upward and the low-frequency roll-off improves with added echo
  pulses, qualitatively correct. A claim of universally “better” filtering would still be too broad because overlap with
  the actual noise spectrum determines coherence.
- **Idealization:** Deep exact zeros and long oscillatory sidelobes imply instantaneous ideal pulses and a fixed timing
  convention. Finite pulse width, pulse errors and experimental bandwidth would alter these curves; state that scope.
- **Logarithmic clipping:** True filter zeros cannot be displayed on a log y-axis. Curves terminate or hit the
  \(10^{-6}\) floor, so the apparent minima are plotting limits rather than residual sensitivity.
- **High-frequency density:** Beyond roughly \(\omega t/2\pi\sim5\), many narrow lobes overlap into a visually noisy
  braid. A zoom/inset, lighter strokes or a narrower x-range would make the main passband comparison easier to retain.
- **Annotation collision:** “DC-dominated: free evolution passes slow noise” touches the top frame and crosses/approaches
  the Ramsey curve. It reads as cramped and risks clipping in alternative renderers.
- **Second annotation:** “passband moves up in frequency with more echo pulses” sits over the CPMG peak without an arrow;
  the intended correspondence is plausible but not precise. Add arrows to Hahn and CPMG maxima.
- **Legend/layout:** The lower-left legend is readable but occupies data space near low-frequency curves; an external or
  compact top legend could reduce interference.
- **Typography:** Axis text is mostly clear, although multiplication/grouping in `noise frequency  ωt/2π` could use
  parentheses and consistent math typography.
- **Source/rendering:** Browser rendering is clean, but the very large sampled path makes diffs and semantic auditing
  difficult. Preserve the generator script and analytical formulas, and use simplification only after error checking.
- **Improvement:** Add provenance and semantic description, define the mathematical convention and pulse locations,
  disclose ideal-pulse/log-floor assumptions, reposition annotations, and consider a focused low-frequency panel.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The moving passband provides a satisfying signal-processing intuition, though the dense
  high-frequency comb becomes more exhausting than illuminating.
- **Completion:** Entire SVG source and browser rendering inspected.

#### `book/part-08-noise-and-qec/figures/lattice-surgery.svg` — source, semantics and rendered appearance

- **Source:** 309-line Matplotlib 3.11.0 SVG arranged as three conceptual panels with mostly live text, simple patch
  rectangles and a hatched seam; it lacks intrinsic accessibility metadata and project generator provenance.
- **Accessibility:** Panel text remains selectable, but no title/description/ARIA reading order narrates the
  merge–measure–split sequence or identifies hatch/color meaning.
- **Sequence:** Separate encoded patches, temporary seam-stabilizer measurement for \(d\) rounds, then release/split and
  retain the classical outcome is the correct high-level shape of lattice surgery.
- **Logical observable:** The red label asserts joint outcome \(\bar Z_1\bar Z_2\). That is correct only for the
  appropriate rough/smooth boundary orientation and merge convention; the generic rectangles show no boundary types,
  data-qubit layout or stabilizer colors that establish it.
- **Distance claim:** Measuring for \(d\) rounds is a useful shorthand for maintaining temporal distance, but actual
  schedules may require \(d\) or a convention-dependent number of syndrome rounds and decoding across space-time.
  Avoid presenting the count as architecture-independent.
- **State evolution:** After a parity measurement and split, the two logical patches are generally projected/correlated;
  they are not simply restored to their independent input states. The visually identical panels (a) and (c) can imply
  nothing happened except obtaining a bit.
- **Correction wording:** “Pauli correction conditioned on outcome” is plausible shorthand, but implementations often
  update a Pauli frame rather than apply a physical correction, and the required frame update depends on the larger
  logical protocol. Say “Pauli-frame update/correction as required.”
- **Fault tolerance omitted:** The figure hides repeated noisy syndrome samples, decoder inference, hook-error-safe
  schedules and changes in stabilizer set. Appropriate for overview, but the caption must call it schematic.
- **Boundary/operation ambiguity:** Lattice surgery is often introduced via both \(ZZ\) and \(XX\) merges. Showing only
  featureless squares may leave readers unable to transfer the picture to the complementary operation.
- **Panel balance:** Headings clearly establish temporal order, and the red hatched seam is visually salient without
  requiring color. Patch labels are legible and unclipped.
- **Label ownership:** The bottom correction sentence begins beneath the gap between panels (b) and (c), so it can look
  like a caption for the whole sequence rather than a post-measurement action. Place it inside panel (c) or connect it
  with an arrow from the recorded outcome.
- **Whitespace:** The wide, shallow three-panel layout is suitable for landscape/full width but leaves large vertical
  whitespace in a browser viewport; intrinsic viewBox itself is acceptably tight.
- **Improvement:** Add semantic metadata/provenance, mark rough/smooth boundaries, call the drawing schematic, show the
  outcome bit flowing into a Pauli-frame update, and state that the post-split logical state has been parity projected.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The merge/split storyboard is intuitive and memorable; one stabilizer-level inset would add
  the missing sense of physical mechanism.
- **Completion:** Entire SVG source and browser rendering inspected.

#### `book/part-08-noise-and-qec/figures/surface-code-lattice.svg` — source, semantics and rendered appearance

- **Source:** 298-line Matplotlib 3.11.0 SVG depicting a \(3\times3\) data-qubit grid, four interior and four boundary
  check regions, two logical strings and a legend; no intrinsic description or regeneration pointer exists.
- **Accessibility:** The blue/orange check distinction is repeated in text labels, but no title/description/ARIA
  semantics provides a reading order, stabilizer supports or non-color encoding within the lattice itself.
- **Code inventory:** “Rotated distance-3 surface code (9 data qubits, 8 checks)” matches the standard parameter count:
  nine data qubits and eight independent stabilizer generators encode one logical qubit.
- **Check inventory:** Four square bulk regions plus four rounded boundary regions visually total eight checks, and the
  alternating X/Z checkerboard is plausible. The drawing does not show which exact data qubits each rounded region acts
  on, however; semicircles visually touch three boundary qubits where rotated-code boundary checks are usually
  weight-two.
- **Potential boundary inconsistency:** The red logical \(\bar Z\) runs horizontally along the bottom row, while its
  label calls it a string “between the Z-free boundaries.” Visually, the left/right boundaries carry orange Z-check
  regions and the top/bottom carry blue X-check regions. The analogous blue \(\bar X\) runs vertically along the left
  column. Under common rough/smooth-boundary conventions, these labels, directions, or boundary coloring appear
  inconsistent; this must be checked against the generator’s explicit stabilizer supports rather than trusted.
- **Commutation audit blocked by abstraction:** A logical string must commute with all displayed stabilizers and the two
  logical strings must anticommute through an odd overlap. Their single corner intersection suggests the latter, but
  the figure’s filled regions are too geometrically ambiguous to verify every stabilizer intersection.
- **Terminology:** “Z-free boundary” is not sufficiently standard or self-defining here. Prefer rough/smooth plus an
  operational statement such as “a Z error string may terminate here,” while acknowledging convention variation.
- **Data/check distinction:** White circles mark data qubits, but the colored faces are labeled “X-check” and “Z-check”
  without showing separate syndrome ancillas. Readers could infer that faces themselves are qubits. State that each
  region denotes a stabilizer measurement/support and ancillas/schedule are omitted.
- **Distance intuition:** The colored logical strings each contain three data-qubit locations, giving a helpful visual
  reason for distance three if their boundary directions are corrected/confirmed.
- **Label collision:** The long red logical-Z label crosses the red string and extends under the lattice; its small type
  and crowded overbar notation are hard to read. The rotated blue logical-X label is likewise small.
- **Legend:** Legend symbols are clear, but face color alone carries X-versus-Z identity inside the lattice. Add `X`/`Z`
  marks or textures for grayscale and color-vision accessibility.
- **Geometry:** Rounded half-plaquettes are visually attractive but imply curved physical connectivity and imprecise
  supports. A conventional rotated-square tiling with explicit weight-two boundary checks would be easier to audit.
- **Improvement:** First verify/correct logical-string orientations and boundary labels from an explicit stabilizer
  table; then add semantic metadata/provenance, exact check supports, non-color X/Z marks, and cleaner logical labels.
- **Entertainment: 4/5.** The compact checkerboard makes topological encoding feel approachable, but the possible
  orientation contradiction undermines the pleasure of discovering the logical strings.
- **Completion:** Entire SVG source and browser rendering inspected; the flagged logical/boundary issue requires
  generator-level verification.

#### `book/part-12-adjacent-models/figures/repeater-chain.svg` — source, semantics and rendered appearance

- **Source:** 326-line Matplotlib 3.11.0 SVG with two stacked process panels, four node boxes, elementary/end-to-end arcs
  and live labels; it has no intrinsic accessible narrative or project regeneration pointer.
- **Accessibility:** Blue and red arcs are also text-labeled, but no title/description/ARIA semantics establishes panel
  order, link direction or the conditional nature of swapping.
- **Elementary links:** Three separately heralded Bell pairs across Alice–\(R_1\), \(R_1\)–\(R_2\) and \(R_2\)–Bob,
  stored until ready, are a correct conceptual repeater-chain starting point.
- **Memory multiplicity:** Each repeater must hold two link qubits (one per neighboring Bell pair). A single node box
  hides this essential local structure and may suggest the same qubit is entangled with both neighbors.
- **Entanglement swapping:** Bell-basis measurements at \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) can project Alice and Bob onto an end-to-end
  Bell state, correct, provided the necessary local qubit pairs and successful elementary links exist.
- **Conditional output:** The final Bell state depends on both two-bit Bell-measurement outcomes. Those classical results
  must reach the endpoints so a Pauli correction/frame can be interpreted; the red arc alone implies an unconditional,
  known Bell state.
- **Timing:** The panel compresses probabilistic asynchronous link generation, heralding latency and memory waiting into
  one instant. State that memories decohere while slower links catch up and that multiplexing/scheduling determine rate.
- **Loss/fidelity:** Swapping extends distance but does not itself purify imperfect pairs; loss, gate/measurement error
  and accumulated infidelity are absent. “Leave Alice and Bob entangled” is idealized and conditional.
- **Operation ordering:** With three ready elementary links, swaps may be organized sequentially or in a nested schedule.
  Drawing both measurement arrows in one panel is acceptable conceptually but should not imply universal simultaneity.
- **Physical versus entanglement links:** Dotted horizontal connections persist in both panels while colored arcs denote
  entanglement. A legend should say whether dotted lines are fiber/classical channels, geography or merely alignment.
- **Visual clarity:** The before/after story is immediately readable, node order is stable, and arc color plus labels
  distinguish local from end-to-end entanglement.
- **Label collision:** “end-to-end Bell pair” lies directly across the red arc near the panel heading, reducing contrast.
  Move it above/below the curve with a white backing or callout.
- **Typography:** Repeater subscripts and two-line Bell-measurement labels become small at normal print width; endpoint
  and node boxes have adequate contrast.
- **Improvement:** Add semantic metadata/provenance, draw two memory qubits per repeater, show classical outcome arrows
  and Pauli-frame dependence, define dotted channels, and label the sequence as idealized/conditional.
- **Entertainment: 5/5.** The local-arcs-to-global-arc transformation is a strong visual payoff and one of the clearest
  storyboards in the asset set.
- **Completion:** Entire SVG source and browser rendering inspected.

### Tracked repository support files — explicit per-file pass

#### `.claude/settings.json`

- **Purpose/correctness:** Valid, minimal tool-specific configuration disables commit and pull-request attribution and
  session URLs, consistent with the repository’s stated public-history preference.
- **Portability:** This is specific to one assistant client and silently has no effect in other tooling. Repository
  policy should live in a human-facing contributor document if it is meant to apply universally.
- **Privacy:** Disabling session URLs reduces accidental disclosure. Empty attribution strings rely on the client’s
  interpretation; a schema/version change could behave differently, so a documented expected result would remove doubt.
- **Maintenance:** Seven lines are clear and contain no secrets. Consider whether a project-wide hidden configuration
  should be tracked at all unless collaborators intentionally share this behavior.
- **Reader entertainment: 1/5.** Pure infrastructure, appropriately terse.
- **Completion:** Entire file inspected.

#### `.gitignore`

- **Coverage:** Sensibly excludes Python caches/environments, common editor debris, build directories and generated
  publication/TeX outputs.
- **Overbreadth:** Global `*.html`, `*.pdf` and `*.epub` rules prevent intentional source fixtures or sample outputs from
  being added without force; directory-scoped build patterns would express intent more precisely.
- **Potential omissions:** Common Python/tool caches such as `.pytest_cache/`, `.mypy_cache/`, `.ruff_cache/`,
  `.coverage` and `htmlcov/` are absent. Add only when the project actually generates them to avoid cargo-cult noise.
- **Build consistency:** Both `book-build/` and `book/_build/` are covered, but any Makefile/build-script output should
  be checked against these exact locations. The tracked `SHA256SUMS` suggests release artifacts are external, reasonable.
- **Safety:** No source-like Markdown, SVG, JSON or Python patterns are ignored, reducing risk of losing authored work.
- **Reader entertainment: 1/5.** Functional and unsurprising.
- **Completion:** Entire file inspected.

#### `BookDescription.md`

- **Role:** A comprehensive positioning/scope document with audience, prerequisites, exclusions, philosophy, goals,
  part summaries, reading paths and market position. It is persuasive and unusually specific.
- **Reconciliation note:** It responsibly declares `book/` authoritative and names known structural drift, but the
  “as of 2026-05-24” date is stale relative to a July 2026 manuscript and obliges maintenance of a long knowingly
  inaccurate description below. Updating the affected Part IV/V passages would be cleaner than preserving corrections
  indefinitely at the top.
- **Scope fidelity:** The thirteen numbered parts match Parts I–XIII; the unnumbered Historical Prelude is omitted from
  the structure and reading paths. Mention it explicitly so readers do not mistake its absence for accidental drift.
- **Audience/prerequisite tension:** “Working knowledge” of eigenvectors, decompositions, tensor products, information
  theory and complexity is a demanding baseline, while the manuscript contains a background/self-check and teaches much
  of this material. Distinguish required fluency from topics the book refreshes to avoid deterring qualified developers.
- **Promise inflation:** Repeated phrases such as “full structured journey,” “understand deeply” and the enormous topic
  inventory can imply textbook-level mastery of every domain. Calibrate the promise toward working literacy where
  chapters necessarily survey rather than derive.
- **Duplication:** Book Description, What This Book Is Not, Core Philosophy, Distinguishing Features, Editorial
  Positioning and Final Summary repeat the same rigorous/no-hype/experienced-developer message. Consolidation could cut
  substantial length without losing identity.
- **Part summaries:** Coverage is concrete and useful for selection, but long comma-separated catalogs read like keyword
  inventories. Each part would be more engaging if led by the problem/question it resolves, followed by fewer exemplar
  topics.
- **Terminology/capitalization:** Capitalizing “Quantum Fourier Transform” in prose is inconsistent with normal generic
  style elsewhere. Acronyms/framework names and claims about current tools also need periodic currency checks.
- **Reading paths:** These are actionable and accurately reference chapter numbers, a strong feature. Algorithms-first
  repeats Chapter 16 after already specifying Chapters 13–17; clarify that it deserves emphasis rather than seeming like
  a sequencing error.
- **Hardware path:** “Chapters 18–22” includes QEC, platforms, control and metrics but omits the explicitly mentioned
  Chapter 24 simulation topic; that may be deliberate, though a hardware/software co-design reader might benefit from
  Chapter 24 as optional.
- **Claims/accuracy:** Statements are predominantly positioning rather than technical assertions. “No dark-ages
  curriculum” is vivid but combative and may date poorly; “modern frontier” content also requires versioned maintenance.
- **Navigation:** The reconciliation note links archive/TOC paths as code spans rather than clickable Markdown links.
  Real links would improve repository use.
- **Reader entertainment: 4/5.** Confident and motivating at first, falling to 2–3/5 through repeated lists. A shorter,
  problem-led description would preserve energy.
- **Completion:** Entire file, including every named section and reading path, inspected.

#### `CITATION.cff`

- **Validity/content:** Compact CFF 1.2 metadata supplies title, message, book type, author, abstract, keywords,
  repository, license, version and release date. YAML structure is clear.
- **Repository precision:** `repository-code` points to the broad `ivoitovych/experiments` repository. If this book lives
  in a subdirectory or has a dedicated canonical URL, cite the most precise stable landing page and add `url`.
- **Version:** `"prereviewed"` is human-readable but not a conventional immutable release identifier. It also appears
  stale after extensive July review work; align it with a tag/edition or explicitly use a prerelease label.
- **Release date:** `2026-07-05` precedes the active review ledger and current edits. If it denotes an actual published
  snapshot, retain it with a matching version/tag; otherwise use the eventual release date rather than the start of
  review.
- **Author identity/privacy:** Name transliteration and public email should be checked for consistency with the desired
  citation identity and privacy policy. ORCID would disambiguate more durably if available.
- **Citation durability:** No DOI, ISBN, preferred citation string or commit/version URL is supplied. Reasonable before
  publication, but archival identifiers should be added for a released book.
- **License:** Declared `CC-BY-NC-ND-4.0` must exactly match `LICENSE` and any repository documentation; later license
  pass should confirm.
- **Reader entertainment: 1/5.** Metadata is not meant to entertain; the abstract remains readable.
- **Completion:** Entire file inspected.

#### `HISTORY.md`

- **Role/coverage:** A 1,247-line chronological engineering narrative from bootstrap through Phase 16. It preserves
  decisions, failures, review methodology, tooling evolution and concrete corrections unusually well.
- **Opening claim:** The assertion that HISTORY, PROCESS and STYLE “do not duplicate” is too absolute. HISTORY repeats
  status ladders, renderer rules, working principles and recurring lessons that necessarily overlap the other two.
  “Serve different purposes, with deliberate overlap” would be more accurate.
- **Chronology:** Numbered phases and dated later programmes provide a strong backbone. Snapshot sections correctly
  describe their historical moment, but readers can easily mistake old counts/statuses for current state; visually mark
  snapshots “historical, not current” and link to `PROGRESS.md`.
- **Stale terminal state:** The pre-Phase-15 “This file will continue…” paragraph presents Phase-14 remaining work as if
  it were the current ending, then Phases 15–16 follow. This was once a conclusion and now interrupts chronology; relabel
  it “Phase-14 outlook.”
- **Phase-16 drift:** It says the second review front is “through Chapter 22 and ~18,000 lines as of this entry.” The
  ledger now covers every manuscript file and all SVGs, so either timestamp that statement more visibly as a phase
  snapshot or append the completed state after this review closes.
- **Internal consistency:** Counts such as 45 initial files, later 47/47, then 48/48 are historically explainable
  (Appendix F, Index, Prelude), but the transitions require inference. A one-line file-count evolution would remove an
  apparent contradiction.
- **Tool/example counts:** Phase 10.4 describes four runnable examples; the current tree has five, and Phase 16 later
  explains the added Qiskit-ordering assertion. Again historically correct, but links or explicit “at that time” wording
  would prevent stale inventory readings.
- **Technical value:** The renderer-bug investigation, arithmetic-correction examples, fact-check freshness/verdict split
  and verify-before-apply discipline are excellent institutional knowledge. They contain enough failure detail to teach,
  not merely celebrate outcomes.
- **Evidence granularity:** Dense commit hashes improve traceability only while rewritten history preserves them. The
  document itself records history rewrites; add stable links/tags or accept that raw short hashes can become dead
  references.
- **Privacy/public positioning:** Phase 16 explicitly narrates an “AI tool” attribution incident and an identity rewrite.
  Given the stated desire to avoid public AI attribution, this prose itself may defeat that policy even though commit
  trailers were removed. The author should decide whether transparent process history or attribution privacy governs
  this paragraph before publication.
- **Voice:** The quoted “aroma of bullshit” and “pure torture” give the history personality and preserve decisive user
  feedback, but they may feel informal or adversarial in a professional public repository. Retain only if that candor is
  an intentional house style.
- **Length/duplication:** The long recurring-lessons section restates many phase lessons almost verbatim. Keeping the
  full narrative is defensible for archival quality, but a generated/current summary plus collapsible phase detail or an
  index would improve retrieval.
- **Navigation:** Paths are often code spans rather than links, and 1,247 lines have no top mini-TOC. Add linked phase
  navigation and direct artifact links.
- **Factual maintenance:** Hardware metrics, tool versions, community issue states and backlog counts are historically
  dated but not uniformly marked in every sentence. A preface that all claims describe the named date/commit would
  reduce accidental present-tense reuse.
- **Reader entertainment: 4/5.** The debugging reversals and methodological discoveries are genuinely engaging; long
  inventories and repeated lessons fall to 2/5. It reads best as an engineering memoir with better navigation.
- **Completion:** Entire file inspected in four sequential ranges, including all 16 phases, snapshots, lessons and
  archival note.

#### `INSTRUCTIONS.md`

- **Purpose:** Clearly states the required author/committer identity and provides verification commands, directly
  addressing the recorded attribution incident.
- **Scope risk:** Requiring every contributor to set the author’s identity makes commits appear authored by Iaroslav even
  when another human contributes. That damages provenance and may conflict with signed-off-by, copyright and platform
  identity expectations. If this is a single-author ghost-editing workflow, say so explicitly; otherwise preserve actual
  authors and control only committer/trailer policy.
- **Global mutation:** Instructing tools/contributors to change `--global` Git identity is unnecessarily invasive and can
  misattribute commits in unrelated repositories. Repo-local configuration is sufficient for this project.
- **Privacy:** The personal email is repeated throughout a public file. Use a verified no-reply/public author address if
  spam/privacy matters, consistently with `CITATION.cff`.
- **Branch wording:** “experimental branch” is vague and may be stale now that the active branch is named
  `quantum-computing-book`. Name the workflow or remove branch-specific wording.
- **Completeness:** Rules cover identity but not commit message style, required checks, pull-before-push, signing or the
  “no attribution trailers/session URLs” policy encoded in `.claude/settings.json`. Either keep the title narrowly about
  identity or centralize all commit policy here.
- **Command safety:** Verification commands are read-only and useful. The distinction between author and committer
  environment variables could be explained for scripted/amended commits.
- **Reader entertainment: 1/5.** Appropriately procedural.
- **Completion:** Entire file inspected.

#### `LICENSE`

- **Identity/match:** Copyright holder, year and `CC-BY-NC-ND-4.0` identifier agree with `CITATION.cff`.
- **License incorporation:** The file paraphrases the Creative Commons deed and links the full legal code rather than
  reproducing it. Make unmistakable that the work is offered under the unmodified official public license and that this
  summary is not a substitute for its legal text.
- **Accurate core grant:** The Share/Attribution/NonCommercial/NoDerivatives/No-additional-restrictions summary closely
  tracks the official deed. The official legal code also expressly permits producing and reproducing (but not sharing)
  adaptations for noncommercial purposes; the local summary could mention this to avoid “NoDerivatives” being read as
  “you may never modify privately.” [Creative Commons legal code](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/legalcode.en)
- **Noncommercial definition:** The local commercial examples are written categorically and extend to any revenue-
  generating product/platform “directly or indirectly.” The official test is whether use is *primarily intended for or
  directed toward commercial advantage or monetary compensation*, a contextual standard. Preserve that controlling
  definition and label examples illustrative, not a unilateral expansion of CC terms.
- **Education ambiguity:** “Private, educational, and other non-commercial use” can imply all education is
  noncommercial; paid courses are later classified commercial. Write “noncommercial private or educational use.”
- **Not fully dual-licensed yet:** The file grants one public license and says a separate commercial license may be
  negotiated; it does not present a second standard license whose terms a reader can accept. “Commercial licensing is
  available separately” is more exact than “This work is dual-licensed.”
- **Attribution scope:** Section 3 says *all* commercial uses must use the suggested attribution, but an individually
  negotiated commercial contract could specify different attribution. Make the separate agreement controlling.
- **Change indication paradox:** The summary requires indicating changes even though modified material cannot be shared
  under this public license. This wording comes from the official deed and can still matter for permitted technical
  modifications; it is not itself an error, but readers may need the legal-code link.
- **Exceptions preserved:** The official license says fair use/fair dealing and other exceptions remain unaffected.
  This local file omits that important notice, potentially making the restrictions look broader than copyright law.
- **Repository scope:** “This work” is ambiguous across manuscript, Python tools, generated figures and third-party
  dependencies. If README promises a manuscript/tooling license split, each path needs a clear license identifier; the
  root file currently appears to cover everything with ND terms, discouraging code contribution/reuse.
- **Warranty:** The local disclaimer is shorter and differently phrased than the official CC limitation. Rely on the
  linked legal code for licensed material; obtain legal review before treating the custom commercial layer as complete.
- **Contact/privacy:** A direct email is functional but should match the author’s chosen public identity/privacy policy.
- **Reader entertainment: 1/5.** Clear for legal prose, though duplicated summaries increase reading burden.
- **Completion:** Entire file inspected and its public-license claims checked against Creative Commons’ official deed and
  legal code on 2026-07-20. This is an editorial consistency review, not legal advice.

#### `Makefile`

- **Interface:** Provides discoverable targets for setup, lint, generated status/index/TOC, book build, figures, examples
  and browser-based render checks. Target descriptions and missing-argument errors are generally strong.
- **Dependency reproducibility:** `pip install --upgrade pip` and unpinned `playwright` make setup time-dependent.
  Figure dependencies are delegated to a requirements file, but browser tooling is not locked; use a lock/version pin
  and record the browser revision.
- **Shared-venv sentinels:** `.installed` and `.figures-installed` independently call `python3 -m venv .venv`. This
  usually tolerates an existing environment but creates two partially overlapping setup states. One base-venv target
  plus separate dependency stamps keyed to requirement hashes would be easier to reason about.
- **Stale stamps:** Touch-file sentinels do not invalidate when Makefile or requirements change. A previously configured
  checkout can remain “installed” with obsolete packages.
- **System Python:** Lint/generators/book intentionally use `python3`, while examples/figures use the venv. Document the
  minimum Python version and ensure system-only scripts truly have no undeclared dependencies.
- **`DELETE` subtlety:** `$(if $(DELETE),--delete-gist,)` treats any nonempty value—including `DELETE=0`—as true. The
  help advertises only `DELETE=1`, but validate equality or use an explicit boolean to avoid accidental remote deletion.
- **Remote side effect:** `render-gist` creates a remote secret gist and may preserve it on failure. The Make target
  should state this external side effect prominently and provide a list/cleanup command.
- **Chromium discovery:** `precheck-chromium` depends on Playwright cache directory naming and `$HOME`, selects the first
  lexicographic match, and warns-success if none is found even though the subsequent capture will fail. Query Playwright
  for its executable or fail with a direct remedy.
- **Platform assumptions:** Setup guidance and `sudo ... install-deps` are Debian/Ubuntu-centric, consistent with the
  documented WSL case but not macOS/other Linux. Mark platform scope rather than presenting universal setup.
- **Cleanup mismatch:** `clean-artifacts` says “Delete review screenshots” and removes only
  `.artifacts/screenshots`; generated figure PNG previews elsewhere under `.artifacts/` remain. That may be intentional,
  but a full-clean target or clearer name would help.
- **Destructive command:** `rm -rf .artifacts/screenshots` is tightly scoped and normal, though a variable-free literal
  path should remain invariant.
- **Build contract:** The long `book` help embeds compatible mdBook/plugin versions but does not enforce installation;
  the build script’s self-test must remain the actual guard.
- **Parallelism:** Independent lint/check targets are not bundled into a single `check`/CI target. Add an aggregate that
  runs lint, TOC drift, examples and book self-tests at appropriate cost.
- **Reader entertainment: 2/5.** Comments make infrastructure approachable; otherwise utilitarian.
- **Completion:** Entire file and every target/recipe inspected.

#### `PROCESS.md`

- **Role:** A strong institutional-memory document covering workflow, review pipeline, toolchain, builds, perishable
  claims, screenshots, renderer bugs, decisions, one chapter retrospective and status gates.
- **File-count defect:** “Forty-seven files total” sums 37 chapters + 3 front matter + 6 appendices + Index correctly,
  but omits the Historical Prelude. The final paragraph says all **48** manuscript files were promoted. Update the
  working-method inventory to 48 and name the Prelude.
- **Review-front drift:** The ledger pipeline assumes an active front and forbids fixes ahead of it. The manuscript front
  is now complete; record the transition to repository-support review and eventually close/retire this constraint so it
  does not block later maintenance.
- **Toolchain incompleteness:** The table omits `generate_index.py`, `build_book.py`, `check_examples.py`,
  `generate_figures.py`, `generate_diagrams.py`, retrofit/status utilities and other tracked tools. Either inventory all
  supported tools or label the table “primary workflow.”
- **Make-target mismatch:** `factcheck_lint.py` and anchor checks have no Make targets, so the advertised CI-free
  baseline (`lint`, `book`, `check-examples`) does not verify the fact-check mirror. A single aggregate `make check`
  should encode the actual gate.
- **Build-version currency:** The mdBook compatibility section is precise and appropriately distinguishes verified from
  manifest-inferred pairs, but package versions/pre-release status are temporally unstable. Attach a verification date
  and derive the displayed matrix from `build_book.py`’s `SUPPORTED_PAIRS` to avoid two sources drifting.
- **Install claim:** “Any 0.4.x works” is broader than the one reproduced 0.4.48 pairing and one example patch. Say
  protocol-compatible in principle, with tested versions named, unless an automated matrix verifies the whole minor
  line.
- **Failure policy tension:** The build script “never hard-blocks” mismatched pairs and always attempts a predictably
  incompatible build. A clear diagnostic followed by failure may be faster and less confusing than cascading TOML
  errors, unless exploratory compatibility is an explicit goal.
- **Moving-target inventory:** The hard-coded warning locations are “as of this writing” with no date and will drift.
  Generate the inventory or link a command/output dashboard rather than preserve a manual list.
- **Final-gate paradox:** `final` requires removing moving-target warnings after re-verification, but perishable facts
  remain perishable the day after final. Replace/remove only the sentinel if another dated freshness mechanism continues
  to surface expiry.
- **Screenshot workflow:** The actual-GitHub loop requires commit and push before visual verification, encouraging
  public history for broken renders. Gist rendering is faster but may differ; the document correctly names that open
  uncertainty, though it should record whether it has since been resolved.
- **Gist decision contradiction:** The older 2026-05-12 entry says the tool captures then deletes the gist; the current
  toolchain says it keeps gists by default and `DELETE=1` cleans up. Mark the old behavior superseded to prevent privacy
  mistakes.
- **Secret-gist terminology:** “Secret” means unlisted, not access-controlled. State that anyone with the URL can read
  the content, important for unpublished manuscript text.
- **CI rationale:** “Single author, no external PRs” is a snapshot, not a durable reason to skip automation. Local hooks
  or CI would still catch environment drift and ensure public commits meet stated gates.
- **Decision log order:** It promises newest entries at top and currently obeys that. Two entries share 2026-05-12 with
  no time/order key; harmless but exact chronology relies on surrounding prose.
- **License wording:** The initial “dual-licensed” decision repeats the LICENSE imprecision: a public NC license plus
  negotiable commercial terms is not yet two simultaneously offered standard licenses.
- **Authorship policy:** “All commits authored as Iaroslav” repeats the provenance concern from INSTRUCTIONS and points to
  a personal email. This should be an explicit single-author editorial policy, not a generic contributor convention.
- **Lessons section incomplete:** It specifies one retrospective per chapter when a chapter reaches `reviewed` or
  `final`; all files remain `prereviewed`, so only Chapter 4 is technically consistent. The heading nevertheless implies
  broader coverage—say “retrospectives begin at reviewed” or include programme-level lessons elsewhere.
- **Promotion criteria:** `prereviewed` is tied forever to a particular 2026-07-03 review, not a reusable quality gate.
  Define invariant requirements first, cite that review as the initial qualifying instance second.
- **Independent-review gate:** “Respected” is subjective. Define required expertise, conflict-of-interest disclosure,
  scope and disposition evidence so status is reproducible.
- **Final status:** Final requires closed fact-check cards and rendering but does not explicitly require author approval,
  clean aggregate tests, license/publication metadata, or resolution of review queues. Decide which belong in a release
  gate versus per-file status.
- **Selective-reader value:** The process repeatedly explains *why* conventions exist, which is excellent. Direct links
  and a short current-state header would reduce the cost of finding applicable rules among historical rationale.
- **Reader entertainment: 3/5.** Renderer forensics and decision rationales are engaging; installation details and
  repeated history are necessarily dry.
- **Completion:** Entire 542-line file inspected in two sequential ranges, including every workflow, decision-log entry,
  retrospective and promotion gate.

#### `PROGRESS.md`

- **Generation/inventory:** Correctly lists 48 manuscript Markdown files, including the Historical Prelude, and groups
  them into phases totaling 7+7+5+8+9+12 = 48. All entries consistently show `prereviewed` and full section counts.
- **“Completed” semantics:** Defining completed as `draft` or later is easy to misread as editorial completion, especially
  when every checkbox is checked. Rename the metric “full draft reached” or “draft-complete,” reserving “completed” for
  final/release status.
- **Progress information:** With every file at exactly the same status, the page mainly proves inventory and phase
  mapping. Add counts per lifecycle state and the next promotion gate/backlog to make it useful after drafting.
- **Generated-file notice:** It says how to regenerate but does not warn “generated—do not edit” or record generator
  version/time. A prominent notice would prevent hand edits.
- **Status context:** `prereviewed` has a project-specific meaning not explained here. Link directly to PROCESS’s
  promotion criteria so public readers do not interpret it as independent review.
- **Section counts:** Counts are internally consistent with manuscript status blocks, but “sections drafted” treats every
  H2 equally and says nothing about fact-check closure, review queues, figures or examples. That is acceptable if scope
  is explicit.
- **Ordering:** Phase order serves the drafting method, not the reader’s book order. The intro should say this directly
  and link TOC for reading order.
- **Accessibility:** Checkboxes communicate state redundantly with textual labels, good. Long lists remain scannable.
- **Links:** Relative manuscript links are complete and useful; root navigation back to README/TOC is absent.
- **Reader entertainment: 2/5.** Clear progress telemetry, not narrative.
- **Completion:** Entire generated summary and all 48 entries inspected.

#### `README.md`

- **Landing-page outcome:** Strongly communicates audience, scope, status, reading paths, rendering/build options,
  project documentation, license and a complete linked TOC.
- **Status candor:** It clearly distinguishes internal `prereviewed` from independent `reviewed` and claim-closed
  `final`, and warns about perishable facts. This is unusually responsible public framing.
- **Scope wording:** “All 37 chapters plus front matter and appendices” omits the unnumbered Historical Prelude and
  Index from the status sentence. Say all 48 manuscript files, then unpack the inventory.
- **Verification nuance:** “External verification of flagged factual claims has been applied” can sound broader than the
  later fact-check caveat. State the finite verified set/pass and explicitly say unflagged claims are not thereby
  certified.
- **Anti-hype pitch:** “without ... physics-first detours” sits awkwardly beside a substantial physics-first Historical
  Prelude and formalism. The intended meaning is probably “without requiring a full physics curriculum”; phrase that
  positively.
- **Prerequisite positioning:** The short prerequisite paragraph is clearer and less intimidating than BookDescription,
  but “operators ... and complexity” may still imply prior mastery. Link the actual self-check as well as the charter.
- **Reading paths:** Practical and concise. All start after/bypass the Historical Prelude without saying it is optional;
  add a one-line Prelude recommendation for history-motivated readers.
- **Runnable-example count defect:** “Project documents” says `examples/` contains four programs, but the tracked
  directory contains five (`qiskit_ordering_check.py` is the fifth). The earlier reading paragraph more accurately says
  code listings in four chapter groups, though it could distinguish embedded examples from the executable convention
  assertion.
- **Build instructions:** Helpful but prominent, version-sensitive troubleshooting occupies a large fraction of the
  reader landing page and duplicates PROCESS. Prefer the tested stable command plus a link to the matrix.
- **Version currency:** “Currently pre-release” is undated and will stale. Generate this claim from the build support
  matrix or stamp the verification date.
- **Installation behavior:** `cargo install mdbook` without a version on the alternative path can install a future
  incompatible line even though the table says 0.5.x. The command should constrain `>=0.5,<0.6` if that is the intended
  pair.
- **License precision:** Calling the manuscript “dual-licensed” repeats the root-license issue; commercial terms are
  available by negotiation, not actually supplied as a second license here.
- **License scope gaps:** “everything under book/ and the prose documents” does not enumerate which root/docs/reviews/
  archive/factcheck prose is covered. Examples and `figures-src/` are also absent from the code/tooling parenthetical.
  Add path-specific license files or a complete scope table.
- **All-rights-reserved tooling:** Publicly exposing reproducibility tools while reserving all rights makes reuse and
  external contribution legally uncertain. This may be intentional, but it conflicts with the collaborative signals of
  a source repository and deserves an explicit choice.
- **TOC:** All 48 manuscript entries are present, ordered logically and linked. Duplication with generated `TOC.md` is
  controlled by `--check-readme`; retaining a compact landing TOC is defensible.
- **Navigation density:** Project-document bullets are long and the full TOC dominates the lower page. A short “Read
  online / Build / Verify / Contribute” quick-action block could improve first-screen utility.
- **Reader entertainment: 4/5.** The opening is energetic and the paths invite exploration; build troubleshooting and
  exhaustive TOC shift into reference mode.
- **Completion:** Entire 223-line file inspected, including every project link, build command, license statement and all
  48 TOC entries.

#### `SHA256SUMS`

- **Coverage:** Contains 192 sorted path/hash records—every currently tracked file except `SHA256SUMS` itself. Excluding
  the checksum file avoids a self-referential digest and is correct.
- **Verification result:** `sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS` on 2026-07-20 reported 191 `OK` entries and exactly one expected
  failure: the active review ledger, which has been appended since the snapshot. This proves all other tracked content
  still matches the recorded snapshot byte-for-byte.
- **Snapshot semantics:** The file has no header, timestamp, commit hash, generation command or stated purpose. Readers
  may mistake it for a current release manifest and see the active-ledger failure as corruption. Pair it with a signed
  release/tag or a README explaining the immutable snapshot it attests.
- **Mutable-file problem:** Including a deliberately insert-only, actively changing review ledger guarantees the manifest
  goes stale on every append. Either regenerate only at declared checkpoints/releases or exclude active audit logs from
  a “source-tree identity” manifest.
- **Generation:** No tracked script/Make target visibly owns this file. Add deterministic generation/check commands that
  use null-safe path handling and a stable locale/order.
- **Security model:** SHA-256 detects accidental/content drift but an attacker able to change repository files can also
  change this unsigned manifest. For release integrity, sign the manifest/tag and publish it through an independent
  trusted channel.
- **Path format:** GNU two-space text format is standard and all current paths are simple; newline/backslash edge cases
  would need care if filenames become exotic.
- **Reader entertainment: 1/5.** Pure integrity metadata.
- **Completion:** Entire 192-line manifest inspected and every recorded digest checked against the working tree.

#### `STYLE.md`

- **Role:** Concise, actionable source-of-truth for layout, chapter structure, math escapes, notation, language,
  Markdown, cross-references, diagrams and authorship.
- **Universal wording:** “Follow them in every file” is immediately qualified by Historical Prelude exceptions and does
  not fit archive/review/factcheck/tool documentation. Scope it to current manuscript source unless repository prose is
  intentionally included.
- **Path template:** `book/part-XX/.../NN-...md` excludes front matter, back matter and the unnumbered Prelude; those are
  described next, but “one chapter” terminology should explicitly handle the Prelude.
- **Renderer mismatch:** The Math section says compatibility with “mdBook + MathJax,” while PROCESS/README/build use
  build-time **KaTeX** via `mdbook-katex`. This is a concrete documentation defect and matters because supported macro
  behavior differs.
- **Pandoc claim:** “Render natively on all” GitHub, mdBook and Pandoc is strong without a tracked Pandoc build/test.
  Either add one or label Pandoc best-effort compatibility.
- **Chapter structure/exceptions:** The normal heading→status→nav→sections→nav contract is clear, and exceptions are
  carefully adjudicated. The exception list is coupled manually to `MERGED_OR_NO_BRIDGE`; tests should prove STYLE and
  lint remain synchronized.
- **Bridge requirement:** Mandating a bridge in nearly every chapter creates formulaic endings, which the manuscript
  review repeatedly assessed individually. The documented no-bridge/merged exceptions soften this, but future decisions
  should remain reader-led rather than lint-led.
- **Status count:** Counting only numbered H2s makes generation deterministic but under-reports substantial unnumbered
  source notes/timelines. Rename the field “Numbered sections drafted” if it remains public.
- **Prelude formatting:** The line beginning “this repository” loses the surrounding list indentation, a small source
  formatting/readability defect even if Markdown continues the paragraph.
- **Math escape portability:** The doubled-backslash workarounds are empirically tied to GitHub’s parser and may produce
  different results in other pipelines; build-time normalization is carrying hidden complexity. Golden render tests
  should cover all target renderers.
- **Inline matrix:** The canonical bug memo/lint reportedly forbids inline `pmatrix`, but STYLE’s Math bullets never state
  that rule directly. Add it so authors do not need to discover it only through lint.
- **Table norm hazard:** PROCESS names table-cell norm bars as a known bug/future lint item, while STYLE merely says
  “avoid heavy math.” State the concrete unsupported pattern.
- **Equation numbering:** Manual numbers such as `(1.3.1)` have no linkable anchors and can drift. Use them only if
  cross-references are linted or avoid numbering.
- **Identity notation defect:** “Identity: `I` (single-qubit) or `I_n` (n-qubit)” can be read as \(I_n\), the
  \(n\times n\) identity, whereas an \(n\)-qubit identity is dimension \(2^n\). Define whether the subscript denotes
  qubits or dimension and use \(I^{\otimes n}\)/\(I_{2^n}\) where ambiguity matters.
- **Qubit-ordering prose:** The decision-log shorthand “Qiskit is little-endian” compresses several separate diagram,
  tensor, integer and printed-bit conventions that the manuscript itself carefully distinguishes. Link the executable
  assertion and avoid the blanket label.
- **Language evidence:** The American-English choice is documented and mechanically enforced. Claims about whole-field
  convention and named title spelling are argumentative detail better kept in the analysis; STYLE only needs the
  decision, scope and exceptions.
- **Optional linter layer:** Behavior changes depending on whether `codespell` is installed, so two contributors can both
  run `make lint` and receive different coverage. Pin/install it or report reduced-mode lint conspicuously.
- **Markdown semantics:** Recommending code spans for “symbols” can conflict with mathematical symbols that should be
  accessible/rendered as math. Clarify code identifiers/gate names versus variables/operators.
- **Self-contained sections:** The signpost-not-prerequisite rule is reader-centered and valuable, but absolute
  self-containment can create repetition and inconsistent local definitions. Define the minimum survival context rather
  than requiring every technical dependency inline.
- **SVG accessibility:** Requiring Markdown alt text is necessary but generated SVGs themselves lack `<title>/<desc>`;
  detached/directly opened assets remain inaccessible. Add intrinsic metadata to generator requirements.
- **Figure provenance:** The pipeline identifies authoritative scripts and previews, good. Add deterministic-generation
  and visual-approval requirements plus supported-width/contrast checks.
- **Authorship:** The final rule repeats the questionable practice of assigning every commit to one identity regardless
  of actual contributor and publishes a personal email. Reconcile with a provenance-safe contribution policy.
- **Reader entertainment: 3/5.** Clear, purposeful rules read well; exception catalogs and renderer escape mechanics are
  dense but useful.
- **Completion:** Entire 209-line file inspected, including all local exceptions and every convention group.

#### `TOC.md`

- **Generation:** Clearly marked as generated by `scripts/generate_toc.py`, names the regeneration target and preserves a
  link to the original plan. This is good generated-artifact hygiene.
- **Major reading-order defect:** The document orders **Back Matter immediately after Front Matter**, before the
  Historical Prelude and Parts I–XIII. The README correctly puts Back Matter last. The generator likely follows path
  sorting where `99-back-matter` precedes `part-*`; encode semantic reading order explicitly.
- **Coverage:** All 48 manuscript files and their H2 headings appear, including unnumbered Prelude timeline/source notes
  and Index letter groups. The table is substantially more complete than README’s chapter-only TOC.
- **Purpose tension:** At 632 lines, it is an exhaustive heading inventory rather than a navigational overview. That is
  useful, but a compact part/chapter index at top would help readers choose before scrolling through hundreds of links.
- **Anchor correctness:** Generated anchors plausibly follow GitHub slug rules for punctuation, apostrophes, en dashes,
  plus signs and starred notation. These are fragile (`Clifford + T` yields a double hyphen; `T2*` loses `*`); an actual
  anchor-resolution test, not only heading-text drift, is required.
- **Cross-renderer anchors:** GitHub, mdBook and Pandoc can slug punctuation differently. The generated TOC targets GitHub
  explicitly but is included in the offline book; build-link validation must rewrite/verify every fragment there too.
- **Index letters:** Omitting unused alphabet letters is reasonable and accurately reflects generated headings.
- **Status/nav omission:** The TOC intentionally excludes status blocks and lower-level H3/H4 headings. State H2-only
  scope so “every section heading” is not interpreted as all heading levels.
- **Chapter closings:** The inventory makes asymmetry visible: some chapters end without Bridge headings per STYLE’s
  adjudications. Generated truth is preferable to forcing uniformity.
- **Terminology:** Back Matter being singular in heading while containing six appendices and Index is conventional.
  Front/Back order aside, part titles agree with README.
- **Reader entertainment: 3/5.** Topic titles advertise the book’s breadth and invite browsing; exhaustive nesting and
  the misplaced appendices weaken flow.
- **Completion:** Entire 632-line generated file inspected in two sequential ranges, including every file/section entry.

### Archive — explicit per-file pass

#### `archive/README.md`

- **Purpose:** Clearly declares the directory frozen, non-manuscript and provenance-oriented, then maps each archive
  group to its current successor.
- **“Superseded” nuance:** Earlier reviews and alternate drafts are not merely obsolete versions; they preserve rejected
  ideas and review evidence. “Not authoritative; retained as historical inputs” is more precise.
- **Navigation:** All referenced paths are code spans rather than clickable links. Convert the delivered Prelude,
  comprehensive review, original TOC and generator references into links for archival exploration.
- **Freeze enforcement:** “Frozen” is policy only; no lint/check prevents edits. `SHA256SUMS` provides a historical byte
  snapshot but is not tied explicitly to this promise.
- **Date/context:** Archive date and original-location explanation are useful. A commit/tag identifier would make the
  relocation event independently traceable.
- **License/privacy:** The archive may contain alternate prose, reviewer text and names under an unclear license scope;
  public-retention policy should cover these artifacts explicitly.
- **Reader entertainment: 2/5.** Brief and helpful; the actual historical interest lives in the linked files.
- **Completion:** Entire file inspected.

#### `archive/chapter0-drafts/chapter0_attempt1.md`

- **Overall:** A compact seven-section causal history with a strong “failed classical test suite → new primitives →
  computational resource” spine. It is clearly superseded but remains useful evidence of the Prelude’s early design.
- **Opening:** The developer/type-system framing is effective, though “Why are states vectors?” is a grammatical error
  (“state vectors” or “states represented by vectors”). The opening also bundles measurement realism and tensor-product
  nonseparability into the classical assumptions broken by the earliest radiation/atomic crises, compressing distinct
  later evidential arcs.
- **§0.1:** Black-body, spectra, photoelectric effect and atomic stability make a vivid failure cluster. Historically,
  “classical reasoning predicted ... ultraviolet catastrophe” needs nuance: the Rayleigh–Jeans divergence and its name
  were articulated around/after Planck’s work, not simply the single calculation that directly caused his 1900 step.
- **§0.1:** Photoelectric threshold language is pedagogically clean but omits emission delay/work function and the fact
  that intensity affects electron count above threshold. Fine for a prelude, but “does not compensate in the classical
  way” is safer than implying intensity never matters.
- **§0.1:** The failed-assertion list includes “measurement reveals pre-existing properties” and nonreducible composites,
  which were not established by the four phenomena just narrated. This is a causal overreach later repaired by the
  EPR/Bell arc.
- **§0.1 entertainment: 5/5.** “Failed assertions in the classical test suite” and “compatibility layer” are memorable
  without becoming gimmicks.
- **§0.2:** Heisenberg/Schrödinger/Born/uncertainty/Bohr/Dirac/von Neumann sequence is coherent. “The state ... is no
  longer a list of definite hidden values” presents an interpretation stronger than the operational Born rule; hidden-
  variable completions are constrained, not excluded merely by Born’s proposal.
- **§0.2:** “Some pairs ... cannot be simultaneously assigned arbitrary precise classical values within the quantum
  formalism” is much better than disturbance-only folklore, but it mixes preparation uncertainty with value assignment;
  later Bell/contextuality evidence should carry the ontological claim.
- **§0.2:** The API analogy is accessible and the six-item formal-language summary earns its place. Calling every state a
  vector ignores mixed states introduced in the same historical paragraph via density operators.
- **§0.2 entertainment: 4/5.** Fast-moving and conceptually satisfying, slightly list-heavy at the end.
- **§0.3:** EPR→Schrödinger→Bell→Aspect→resource reversal is the strongest narrative unit. “Strongly supported quantum
  predictions over local hidden-variable models” is defensible, while loophole closure/detection assumptions deserve a
  dated sentence in a publication-grade version.
- **§0.3:** The resource list risks implying entanglement is necessary for every named algorithmic speedup; “some” helps,
  but the relationship is more nuanced than the rhetorical reversal suggests.
- **§0.3 entertainment: 5/5.** The paradox-to-resource reversal has genuine drama.
- **§0.4:** Turing/Shannon/Landauer/Bennett/Wiesner/BB84 forms a useful independent strand. “Erasing information has
  thermodynamic cost” should specify logically irreversible erasure and the ideal lower bound \(k_BT\ln2\).
- **§0.4:** “For a while ... independent of physics” is rhetorical history; abstraction never implied literal physical
  independence. The section later corrects this, but “allowed engineers/theorists to abstract away substrate” is more
  exact.
- **§0.4:** The slogan “If information is physical, and the physical world is quantum...” is motivating but not a proof
  that classical computation is inadequate; classical models can simulate finite quantum systems with overhead.
- **§0.4 entertainment: 4/5.** The return of physics is a compelling second-act structure.
- **§0.5:** The Benioff/Feynman/Deutsch progression is clear. “Benioff made ... possible. Feynman made it necessary.
  Deutsch ... universal” is excellent rhetoric but historically/technically overabsolute: no theorem made quantum
  computers necessary, and universality has model/approximation qualifications.
- **§0.5:** “An (n)-component” contains stray parentheses and conflates component count with qubit-local dimension; use
  an \(n\)-qubit system and \(2^n\)-dimensional state space.
- **§0.5:** “State may contain many amplitudes” should avoid information-storage implications; the next measurement
  sentence helps, but amplitude-description size is not directly extractable memory.
- **§0.5 entertainment: 5/5.** The possibility/necessity/universality triad is memorable despite needing qualifiers.
- **§0.6:** The oracle-algorithm progression is accurate at overview level. Deutsch–Jozsa’s query advantage must remain
  explicitly exact/deterministic-classical; the draft does name deterministic classical but not the exact/promise
  comparison.
- **§0.6:** Shor’s deployed-cryptography stakes, Grover’s quadratic boundary and QEC reversal are well chosen. “Fault-
  tolerance theory showed arbitrarily long computation” requires standard assumptions: local stochastic noise,
  scalable fresh ancillas/control and threshold/model conditions.
- **§0.6:** The bit/phase/code discussion avoids no-cloning misconceptions well but skips the chronology and syndrome
  mechanism that make QEC’s discovery feel concrete.
- **§0.6 entertainment: 5/5.** The sequence of escalating stakes and “how much engineering?” turn is highly effective.
- **§0.7:** The recap is clean and returns to the reader contract. It repeats the opening thesis almost verbatim and
  could close with a more concrete handoff rather than a third “engineering order” statement.
- **§0.7 entertainment: 4/5.** Strong synthesis, slightly over-recapped.
- **Archive hygiene:** It has no explicit “superseded/not authoritative” banner inside the file; direct links/search
  landings can expose old claims without archive context. Add a frozen header if archival files remain public.
- **Completion:** Entire 213-line alternate draft inspected section by section.

#### `archive/chapter0-drafts/chapter0_attempt2.md`

- **Overall:** A substantially expanded 12-section/4-Era draft with stronger chronology, dependency tags and a final
  assumption/replacement table. It contains much of the delivered Prelude’s eventual architecture but also preserves
  several rhetorically attractive overclaims.
- **Opening correctness:** “The postulates ... are not axioms” is a category error. They are axioms/postulates *within
  the formal model* even though experiment and theory selection motivate them. Nor does each map cleanly to one
  experiment or theorem; tensor composition and unitarity are broader structural commitments.
- **Opening contract:** Optionality, selective-reader payoff and exclusions are unusually clear. Calling the chapter
  “load-bearing” later in §0.9 conflicts with “nothing here is load-bearing for the mechanics”; distinguish conceptual
  motivation from prerequisite status.
- **Opening entertainment: 4/5.** Confident and inviting, though repeated “this chapter” process prose delays history.
- **§0.1 accuracy:** “The fit ... was ... exact” overstates every empirical theory’s domain and precision. The familiar
  end-of-century complacency story is historiographically contested; acknowledge active foundational problems rather
  than assigning a universal mood.
- **§0.1 structure:** Pairing ether failure with black-body radiation neatly locates two revolutions, but ether is then a
  narrative cul-de-sac. The developer bug analogy is memorable and appropriately says classical physics did not fail
  everywhere.
- **§0.1 entertainment: 4/5.** Strong analogy and tension, slightly too polished into a single inevitability narrative.
- **§0.2 category defect:** It promises “four measurements,” but atomic stability is a theoretical inconsistency, not a
  measurement, and Rutherford’s 1911 nuclear model sits just outside “roughly 1860–1910.” Say four empirical/theoretical
  crises.
- **§0.2 history:** Rayleigh–Jeans/equipartition does produce ultraviolet divergence, but the retrospective “catastrophe”
  narrative postdates Planck’s 1900 law and should not imply Planck simply reacted to their final derivation.
- **§0.2 photoelectric detail:** Above threshold, intensity primarily changes photocurrent while maximum kinetic energy
  follows frequency in the ideal account; “not their energy” needs experimental/saturation qualifications.
- **§0.2 synthesis:** Discreteness is a productive common thread, but it does not alone explain atomic stability,
  contextual measurement or the later state formalism. The diagnosis is too singular.
- **§0.2 entertainment: 5/5.** The four-crisis test suite is exceptionally readable.
- **§0.3 Planck:** “Oscillators ... exchange energy only in discrete units” is serviceable history, but Planck’s original
  energy-element interpretation and later resistance were subtler than “formal trick to make the sum converge.”
- **§0.3 Einstein:** The 1921 Nobel Prize was presented in 1922; saying “awarded ... in 1921” conventionally names the
  prize year but can confuse chronology. “Explained ... completely” overstates the early theory and later material/work-
  function understanding.
- **§0.3 models:** Calling Bohr’s model “from first principles” contradicts the paragraph’s admission that its central
  rules were postulated. It derived Balmer/Rydberg behavior from a hybrid model, not from established first principles.
- **§0.3 Stern–Gerlach:** The silver-beam split was only later understood through electron spin; calling it the direct
  physical ancestor of a qubit is evocative but anachronistic and platform-specific.
- **§0.3 entertainment: 5/5.** The compatibility-layer/rewrite arc has excellent momentum.
- **§0.4 noncommutativity:** It is central but not “the algebraic source of nearly everything” quantum, and noncommuting
  observables do not imply that every measurement of one necessarily disturbs every state/property of the other.
- **§0.4 Born/ontology:** “Full wavefunction, with no hidden missing information” and “not hidden classical properties”
  declare completeness beyond the operational Born rule. Bell/contextuality constrain hidden-variable theories later;
  this paragraph should not settle interpretation in 1926.
- **§0.4 uncertainty:** Noncommutativity alone does not mean two observables can never both be sharp; noncommuting
  operators can share particular eigenvectors, and the Robertson bound depends on the state/commutator expectation.
  Use the specific canonical position–momentum relation or a compatibility qualification.
- **§0.4 Dirac:** The relativistic equation’s negative-energy solutions led to the positron prediction through a more
  complicated historical interpretation than “a particle identical ... oppositely charged”; concise wording is fine if
  it avoids presenting the modern antiparticle picture as immediate.
- **§0.4 entertainment: 5/5.** Interfaces/representations make the formal revolution unusually approachable.
